div.head: YARD,
div.p: YARD,

A Busy Time. February is a very important month in the poultry yard. As a matter of fact, this and the succeeding month are undoubtedly the most im- portant of the whole year, and if the next few weeks are allowed to slip away without their being taken full advantage of, the loss cannot be rectified for another twelve months. During February next winter's laying stock should be hatched, since these birds are generally of the heavy, general purpose type, and take a good many months to reach a laying age. The aim should be to have the hens beginning to lay by November Ist, as in this case, with careful treat- ment and regular feeding, they will probably continue throughout the winter months. If they are much later than this in commencing to lay, no eggs may be looked for until well into the new year, while, on the other hand, if they commence earlier than about November Ist, they will cease immediately the really cold -weather sets in. The exact age at which a pullet begins to lay depends upon quite a variety of circumstances; it depends on the breed, on the strain, on whether the birds are forced or allowed to develop naturally; ad it depends to some extent :upon the season, some years' development being slower than others. This last point, however, can be largely gOverned by the treatment, and so is not a very important feature. The date of this year's hatching should be noted as well as the time the pullets begin to lay, ,and the time must be altered accordingly next spring.

The Breeding Pen. The temptation this year to sell eggs for hatch- ing is not so great as in normal times, since prices for new-laids are so extraordinarily high, Still, if one possesses good stock it pays well to advertise any surplus eggs that one may have in the agricultural and poultry papers. To obtain a good price the parent stock, of course, must be true to type and of good quality. The demand during February for eggs for hatching purposes is very great indeed, and when the breeding pen is composed of reliable and true-to- type birds there is little difficulty in selling the eggs at a good price. This is one of the reasons why I am so great a believer in pure-bred stock rather than mongrels. The former cost- no more to feed or house, and yet their produce can be disposed of for twice, sometimes twenty times, as much money. If the stock birds are mongrels or cross-breds—very different terms, by the way —their eggs do not realise more than an eating price; they are of little use for hatching pur- poses. Rill of the utmost importance when pro- ducing eggs for incubation that they shall con- tain strong germs. Now the season is fairly well advanced, the proportion of hens to male birds may be materially increased. With bens of the laying or non-sitting clliss, provided they have their liberty, as many as a dozen may be run with each cock, while with those of the heavy type about two-thirds of this number is sufficient.

The Colony Plan. • Whenever the conditions allow, it is an excel- lent plan to house the birds in portable sheds, scattered far and wide about the fields, allow- ing them full freedom to .wander about all day long. The advantages of this colony system are many; the birds are healthier, they are much cheaper to maintain as they find a large quantity of food for themselves.

div.head: SULPHATE OF AMMONIA.
div.p: SULPHATE OF AMMONIA.

Lord Selborne desires to call the attention of farmers to the fact that the decision to suspend the issue of licences for the export of sulphate of ammonia was based on the assumption that the home demand for this fertiliser would be substantially increased. Unless, therefore, farmers at once increase their demand, the re- sult will be that stocks will accumulate and the output will be curtailed. In view of the importance of using every effort to stimulate the production of maximum crops during the war, in the interests both of agriculture and of the nation generally, Lord Selborne appeals to farmers to avail themselves without delay of the present opportunity to procure supplies of sulphate of ammonia for spring use. Leaflets dealing with the use of sulphate of ammonia may be obtained free of charge on appliCation to the Secretary, Board of Agricul- ture and -Fisheries, 8, Whitehall-place, Loudon, S.W.

div.head: WOMEN FARM WORKERS.
div.p: WOMEN FARM WORKERS.

The Board of Trade, in consultation with the Board of Agriculture, are taking active steps to mobolise a sufficient supply of women for work on the land in order to meet the scarcity of agricultural labour due to the enlistment of men in His Majesty's Forces. The reserves of women's labour available for agriculture are to be found chiefly among the local unoccupied women in country villages, who have some ex- perience of or familiarity with agricultural work, and also among the better educated women who are willing to be trained for this purpose. Speakers are to be provided to address meetings on the subject in different parts of the country, more women organisers have been appointed, and a house to house can- vass will be made with a view to induce women in rural districts to offer their services as farm workers.

NO UNCULTIVATED LAND IN FRANCE. The French Government have resolved upon strong measures for the organisation of agri- culture during the war. The 'Minister of Agri- culture, M. &feline, has introduced a Bill pro- viding for the compulsory cultivation of abandoned land, and otherwise to ensure the full development of the country's resources in the present year and till peace has been restored. In presenting the measure M. Melina stated that there was a deficiency of 10 per cent. in the area under crop last year, the reduction in wheat alone amounting to 475,000 hectares (about 1,187,000 acres), presumably including the pro- vinces held by the enemy. The loss of the north-eastern districts reduces considerably the acreage available, and if the country is to be self-supporting there muot be jrater concen- tration of effort in the rein6.ining departments. The Bill provides that- a- fortnight from the premulgatiOn of the Government order the mayor of each commune, assisted by two muni- cipal councillors, shall call Upon the Owner and the usual cultivator of any land left unculti- vated for any reasorl whatever to put his land under crop. If within another fortnight work has not been begun, the maybr shall have the right to requisition such land and hand it over for cultivation to a local committee for agri- cultural operations constituted by the decree. The mayor shall have the right to requisition for the work any available implements, draught animals, 'and buildings.--" Field."

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
SHALLOTS.

It is surprising how popular these are with cottagers and allotment holders. The old true shallot and the large red or Jersey are equally well grown. Many of the growers like them for ordinary flavouring, while others prefer to pickle them, more especially the smaller true shallot. This, if the ground is rich comes not only of good size but in large clusters and very, clean. They should when well grown wear a satiny aspect. For home use the true shallot is far more worth growing than the large red. Planted now if the ground is in good condition in rows 12 inches apart growth soon follows, and the produce is early ripened and can be cleared off.

div.head: WINTER GREEN STUFF.
div.p: WINTER GREEN STUFF.

All winter green stuff, such as Brussels sprouts, savoys, and coleworts seems to be very luxuriant, and sappy, hearting or otherwise turning in long before they are wanted. Should we have no severe weather no harm will follow, but we must not expect to get through the winter with- out some severe frosts, a few of which would do these coarse, sappy, greens great harm. Those who planted late, say in. August and September so as to have them coming in when most needed, will fare the beet.

div.head: POTATOES.
div.p: POTATOES.

A friend writes to me that he has had great difficulty with his potatoes this year in regard to the quality. In many cases I fear the cooking has much to do with this failure, although in justice it must be said that the best cook in the world would fail to render some potatoes fit for the table. As a case in point I purchased some King Edwarei VII., which on being cooked were what is termed soapy and very inferior. From another source I procured some of the same variety, and the difference was most marked. The latter .were when cooked mealy and of ex- cellent quality. ' In fact they A, wanted the greatest care when being boiled, otherwise they would have broken down into pulp. Those who have to purchase most of thcir potatoes from the greengrocer are to a certain extent helpless, as it is very difficult whTn one gets a good potato to purchase the same sort a seoond time. In the case of those who grow their own potatoes there is no reason, seeing the enormous number of sorts now available, that is, best as regards quality and; best suited to the soil. There is no doubt in my mind that soil has much to do with the quality of potatoes.—Wick, in "Farm and Home."

Handicapped. Perhaps readers will suffer a personal note at the outset. Since I last wrote I have had a painful mishap. Result: an ugly wound on the left leg, which threatens to keep me indoors for some time. While (if with due modesty I may so express it) ply right hand has not "forgot her cunning," my unfortunate accident has put me somewhat at a disadvantage; hence this fore- word. • I chabod.

Monday wp the feast of St. Valentine, but its glory has departed; though some of us old fogeys vi7ell remember a period when it was held in considerable ' repute, it rapidly faded and dwindled ere the Victorian age gave place to the unsentimental twentieth century, and lovers no longer exchange the "elaborate confections in paper lace, with rosy cupids and hearts entwined and transpierced " which on this anni- versary thrilled with delight the hearts of their mothers, and particularly of their grand- mothers. For St. Valentine's Day, now of no account at all, dates back to the beginning of the third century. .;

Anniversary Fragment I am glad to thinkf I am now on sufficiently intimate terms with regular readers of this column to mention that I was married on a Valentine's Day. How long ago, let me indicate thus:—
Lo, here ! The fortieth milestone on the road That all who enter must by Hymen's gate Let's rest on't, and, with reminiscent gaze, E'en chew the cud of mempry fond a-while.
That this road hath its ups and downs is true— As what highway hath not rough parts with

Tit-bits.

In last week's competition in the "Children's Corner" one little nephew admitted a prefer- ence for an encyclopmdia. I was somehow re- minded of an incident once narrated by Sir Walter Scott, but probably forgotten by many readers. An old farmer, who had 'called on a matter of business, was. shown into the library to wait a few minutes. Sir Walter snrprised him in the act of poring over a dictionary, and asked how he liked the book. " A-weel,"' was the reply of the cautious Scot, "they're vera pretty stories,,,but they're unco' shor-r-t." An Organ Experience.

Last week's reference to the Orford Parish Church organ project reminded me of .a singular occurrence in a district in which I once lived. After vain attempts to patch up an old organ at a Mission Church, the curate-in-charge as un- successfully tried to sell it, although his original price of £BO gradually came down to £26. He then had it removed to an adjacent field and made a bonfire of it! He next applied for a Carnegie grant for a new instrument, but that Cock • would not fight either. Ultimately, a wealthy widow presented an organ in memory of her deceased husband. "Uncle Tom's Cabin."

Reverting to the competition on "Books chil- dren like—and why," I confess I was surprised on learning that at least one of the younger generation was familiar with and fond of this work. When I was the age of the niece in question, "Uncle- Tom's Cabin" was the only book I possessed, and I read and re-read it alternately with thg " ProgreSs," borrowed from a neighbour. I think that even now I could pass an examination in either or both of these. ' " Box " Brown.

I wonder how many old Warringtonians re- member this personage. Five-and-fifty years have passed since I met him, so they must be comparatively few. He was an American negro, who, born in slavery, claimed to have gauged the possibilities of man's inhumanity to man, having in his own person suffered barbarities which were a disgrace to the vaunted civilisa- tion, not to mention the supposed Christianity, of the perpetrators. When a little later I received ' a copy of the famous " Cabin " as already stated (in all likelihood, not for the first time, but perhaps in the circumstances the reader will not mind) my childish fancy natur- ally pictured " Box " Brown as "Uncle Tom." Of course, there was a point at which the analogy failed; then Brown may be said to have merged into Harris, who also fled from the house of bondage and triumphantly reached the land where men might not buy and sell their brothers as goods and chattels.

Human Freight. Rut why or whence "Box " Brown? Well, as some of my contemporaries may recollect, that bold " cullud pusson," determined at all hazards to be free, contrived tb have himself packed in a box and transhipped as baggage, and so crossed into Canada. Those were the days when domestic slavery, with all its evil, was rife in the Southern States, and "Box" Brown, with his thrilling experiences of cruelty and oppression and Cs exciting adventures, was to us wee folk an attractive personality, and to the com- munity as a whole a heroic figure. Smart Business.

Even so long ago there were travelling enter-, tainers who knew how to "work" a cheap "ad." " Box " Brown was conspicuous among these. But for the Hibernicism, one might conveniently describe him as his own advance' agent. On deciding to pitch his tent at a particular spot for a season, he would make a • tour of the ' elementary schools, enlist the head teacher's sympathy, and dispose of a number of cheap, tickets through, these channels, and so repeatedly pack his house. The mistress in charge of the mixed department, among whose tiny units was my diminutive self, was especially.gracious unto the enterprising man of ebony. At once a descendant of Ham and a son of Anak, if I may so put it, he early found favour with the worthy "school-marm," as was surely meet and right, for she now reappears before my mental vision as if she had stepped out of the frontispiece of an illustrated edition of Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe's once exceedingly popular book—side " corkscrew " cqrls and all " Business as a Science."

Frost represents one of two widely divergent schools of opinion that have long waged war with varying fortunes, and between, which there is no truce. Assuredly his is destined to win, and the war between the nations may well be said to have hastened the .day of assured victory for the practical educationists. Bases.

Another authority I once met insisted upon these as assets which business education should furnish for the accomplishment of a lucrative life work :—First: How .to take that physical exercise necessary to the proper care of the body; because if one falls into ill-health, all things else become insignificant. Second: A knowledge of One's own language. Third: Ability to make analyses. Fourth: A knowledge of the use ,of figures. Fifth: An understanding of the principles of classification and organise.; tion. Beyond, come the courses of "specialisa- tion to fit the student for the work he has elected to pursue." As Mr. -Frost plainly inti- mated, fathers and sons must make up their minds to an adequate period of serious and determined preparation for the latters' business careers, and, once . launched upon them, to continuo to "covet earnestly the best gifts." As .1 read in the "Life and letters of Brooke Foss Westcott ": "It, will be a great help to pause from time to time in the midst of work, and quietly to ask yourself whether it is your best." These disjointed sentences barely indicate my view of these supremely important matters. Plainly no ex- pert, I would fain have added one or two quota- tions in support, but the sands of my hour glass have -once more run nut.

div.head: GIBISIMAS I THE LAST.
div.p: GIBISIMAS I THE LAST.
Corporal Frank Kay Describes The Festival.
ENGLAND PREFERRED.
Corporal Frank Kay, a member of "The Examiner" literary' staff writing home, gives his experience of Christmas and New tear "somewhere in the East." .

"To my mind," he says, "Christmas, in Eng- land is an ideal festival. I don't know whether I should have been so firm in that opinion twelve months ago for, curiously enough, I never realised fully all the beauties of an English Christmas until I missed one. Frankly, I don't want to miss any more. Imagine Christmas on a day in the middle of July, and then you will be able to form an idea of what our Christmas was like out here. What a paradox!. What a Christmas!

"Since the beginning of September I had given up any hopes I might have cherished of being at home for the great joyous festival, and had fully made up my mind to make the best of things; twelve months of soldiering having taught one how to bow to the inevitable with a smile, and without getting pains in the back.

div.head: TIMELY CONCERT.
div.p: A TIMELY CONCERT.

" Alicawber-like, I waited for something to turn up during Christmas week that would brighten things a little, and I must confess I thought the outlook very gloomy, even on the morning of the 24th. At the eleventh hour, or, to be more precise, at 2.30 p.m., the boys in our tent received an invita- tion to a smoking concert to be held at night in the Royal ,Naval Air Service lines. Needless to say, we accepted the invitation with pleasure, and late in the afternoon, when we were in the midst of an elaborate toilet, an observer would have thought that we were going to look on feces very much fairer than those of our hosts, so great Were the pains we were taking. _ We even rubbed .our boots over, and I cannot recall the auspicious occasion on active service when .such pains were deemed necessary before. We meant to create a. good • impression, and evidently our hosts were intent- on the same thing, for exactly at six o'clock a motor 'for the R.N.A.S. concert party " was announced. We got aboard very quickly and were soon bowling along to the concert hall. On the way we de- livered a case of plum puddings at another.depot —a .4. fatigue' for which we were allo*ed an extra half-hour's leave. A huge marquee had been -placed at , the disposal of the concert organisers, and with the limited material in the way of flags and bunting which they had ion hand, they had succeeded in adding a delightful cheeriness to the interior, which, by the way, was lighted by means of motor head-lamps. There was a decent stage, upon which there was a piano, but, no doubt, a timid person would not have been much in favour with the auditorium, for the stalls,' 'pit' and 'circle' seats were made up of _cases of bombs and ammunition.

"The concert opened with a pianoforte solo, executed in skilful fashion by a chief petty officer, and then followed no less than twenty- two items, each of which was excellent, be it humorous, sentimental or instruminital, Oh, yes, there were two or three cornet and violin duets, and the pieces were well chosen and most creditably interpreted. There were several topical tit-bits touching on happenings out here, but which I cannot tell you about as yet, which were received with enthusiasm, and the many popular—Lwon't say old-Tsongs which were ren- dered were enjoyed quite as much as the later melodies. Each artiste gave of his best, and the audience showed its high appreciation by cheering vociferously and by joining heartily in the many choruses. A clever 'stunt' by 'the village curate' caused roars of laughter, no one being offended by the following opening remarks of 'the reverend gentleman ':-- It was my dear mother's wish that I should preach to the heathen, and now, I am ,pleased to say, her -wish has been gratified.' "A farcical boxing contest for a handsome tin of ' bully ' was a 'great success as a mirth provoker. In conclusion the pianist played the National Anthems: of the Allies in masterly. fashion, and cheers were heartily accorded the officers who were present. The motor was wait- ing for our party, and we were driven right down to our depot, where, after wishing the sentries 'a happy Christmas,' and getting a sarcastic laugh in reply, we turned in, having spent a most delightful Christmas evening.

DAINTIES FROM HOME APPRECIATED. "Christmas Day, as I have said, was quite warm, but nevertheless we had made -up our minds to play a football match, and play it we did—although a bathe in the sea might have been more fitting. A Taube paid us a visit shortly after dinner—which, by the way, had included a course of Christmas pudding, pro- yided by the 'Daily News' fund—and so clear was the atmosphere that we could make out distinctly the black Maltese crosses on his planes. The airman dropped bombs, but did not do any damage, and quickly Made off when our guns opened on him. He did not venture across again that day to disturb our peace. At night we spent a jolly time in one of the tents, where a sing-song was in full swing. Each man in the unit had to sing—save the mark—a song, or, if he did not know a whole song, a chorus. The Christmas carols were joined in by the whole company, and the sing-song was voted a great success by all present. I cannot say what was the opinion of those who heard it from out- side, for I never took the trouble to inquire. It's just possible that no one heard it, for we haven't been accused of anything as yet. "The Greeks who are here had evidently heard seasonable greetings passed pretty fre- quently, for on Boxing Day a Greek fireman came to our tent and with quite a Christmassy smile wished us 'A Merry Chtistmas Eve.' We nearly all burst into laughter, but managed to keep ourselves under control until we had cor- dially- returned the greeting and Georgius had gone, quite proud of his knowledge of English and English customs. "Our ChristafaS mails had arrived in good time, and the little dainties which nearly all of us received helped to brighten the season very considerably. They proved that the thoughts of these-in England were with us, despite the fact that we are thousands of miles away; and that in itself is ekceedingly cheering. Those' people who were thoughtful.enough to send something seasonable' to 'Tommy' can rest assured that their gifts brought great happiness, and were fully appreciated. I can vouch for it so far as my observations went.

"On the whole, my Christmas was exceptionally good, in the circumstances, but for preference give me the Christmas with frost and snow, holly and mistletoe, roaring fires and roasting chestnuts. snap dragon and musical chairs—an English Christmas.

div.head: WELL PROVIDED FOR AND NOT DOWNHEARTED.
div.p: WELL PROVIDED FOR AND NOT DOWN- HEARTED.

"We had another sing-song on New Year's Eve and the New Year was heralded in by the shrieking and shrilling a the sirens and whistles on the ships lying off the shore. The; Turks would no doubt wonder what it was, but we knew, and, quickly joining hands, sang 'Auld Lang Sync' with gusto and exchanged , cheery greetings with --each other. On New Year's Day I was assisting in the stores issue marquee cutting up bacon and 'cheese and ' weighing out ,tea and sugar, Ac. On the 2nd of January I got back to my usual work—get- ting in stores from the transports. I have not-. much time to spare when the sea is calm, but when Neptune loses his temper .it is well-nigh impossible to 'carry on.' SoMething must have vexed him now hence my having the time AO write you this long letter. "We are having it pretty cold at present, but we have not had any real winter weather since November, when we had three days of frost, snow and storm—when incidentally I was stranded on -a transport and could not get ashore owing to the "roughness of the sea for three dayS. For the most part the weather is quite mild, for all, the world like autumn weather at home. - "Anyhow we are well provided for; we have had an issue of thick -winter clothing,, and, personally. I received a very useful parceP of comforts from the ladies of St. -John's PreSby- terian Church. Their payed also included cigarettes, a Christmas cake and sweets, and I can assure you I fully appreciated their kind thought. ." As you know, we are not allowed to .men- tion anything as to military movements, so all I can say is that when you get the news please remember that 'We're not downhearted yet.'"

CYCLING AND MOTORING.
Pleasant Social And Charitable' Function In Parr Hall. To improve Mudguards And Make Them Effective.

To the ail-weather cyclist—and this, in one way or another, probably applies to quite 75' per cent. of those who own machines—good mudguards are a necessity, and we find very few roadsters which are not fitted with them. To make mudguards really, effective there are two additions I would suggest, both to the front guard. An extension some nine inches in length, extending from the fork crown over the top of the front wheel prevents the mud being blown- on to the. rider. It is not .an unsightly attachment, but rather adds to the appearance of the,machine, .To hinder the boots becoming muddy, a. pear-shaped •peace Of leather; about seven or eight inches. wide, fastened to the bottom of the front mudguard and corning to within three inches of the ground, is very serviceable. • The two additions are particularly needed by all-weather riders. Many of the best make* now tit these as standard, ,and, frankly,. I would not have &machine without them.

And how did the money come? First, you paid a shilling to go in, and then had afternoon tea- either at a little square or round table, while Mrs. W. B. Roberts's band, on the platform, dis- coursed pleasantly. There were about forty tables, and as many waitresses attired in what- ever dresses they preferred,---their best—Juliet caps, and dainty aprons. They brought tea bread and butter, .scones, and baby. muffins: Supernumeraries paced the red panels of carpet ,placed lengthwise down . the hall, and offered cakes at a penny a time. Immediately in front of the platform stood a stall on which were plants, flowers, fancy goods, &c., and a picture by Mr. Oswald Garside, all given to be sold. It was alleged to have been written by the young and reserved author, Mr. Shernard Baw (it was only a rumour) with the incidental music specially concocted by Sir Bhornas,Teecham. Sir Beafool Free was said to have ,rehearsed the production night and day for the last twelv.3 years. As a matter of fact, the play was a mixture of Mr. Jackson and Mr. McNally, who only finished it at two o'clock on Thursday morning, and gave the artistes no time for rehearsing. The play was all the better ?Or that perhaps, for its novel incongruity struck a humorous chord in the hearts of the spectators. A fair number of sovereigns Were raised in this way. • Later in the crush room Miss Felicia Sutton and her concert party attracted a considerable number of people. "Tell Me Pretty Maiden". was rendered by; 'double quartet party; and Miss Davenport and Miss Molly Shaw ".sang enjoyable solos. In the main hall the selections by Mrs.. Roberts's band were interspersed with various solos—Miss Marie Houghton sang "Annie Laurie," "Seep the home fires burning," "Daddy's Sweetheart," and "For You Alone": the Misses Jones sang "Night of Stars" and "Somewhere a voice is calling,"; Mrs Dallow, " Carmenar and A. N. Other; Mrs. Haviour played a violin solo; Mr. R.. Smith a cornet solo; and Mr. W. H. Rigby sang ." Captain Mac"; and Miss Jessan4 Bryce .danced beau- tifully; '

In the evening. the Band of the 2nd South , Lancashire Regiment, conducted by Mr. H. E. Cahill, rendered interesting selections. Sergt. Lawrence G. Brennan 'sang "The Veteran's „Song"; Miss Marie Houghton sang Tosti's L'Ultima Canzone " (accompaniment spec!all- arranged.for the band by Mr. Cahill); Mrs. E. A. And whO were the committee who promoted the Cafe Chantant? They were a dozen ladies, deeply interested in Red Cross work, who de- sire that their names shall go unrecorded. The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) de- clared the function open, the Rev. H. V. Piga presiding. The Mayor 'hoped that those present would do all they could for the good of the cause. Warrington was very fortunate, indeed, that we had Raddon Court Hospital. It was thv only Red Cross hospital in the town, and whilst he believed we did not generally take much inter- est in the society before the war,. we were doing so now. The ladies were doing a noble work. (Applause.) Captain Mathams proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor, the Chairman, and all who were assisting at the function. Mr. .H. B. Houghton secOnde-d The Captain remarked that when there was so much horror on all sides, it was a fortunate thing that those who could not wear khaki could find an outlet for their energies in Red Cross, 'work. div.head: For Country and Righteousness.
div.p: For Country and Righteousness.

The Rev. James Davies, in "St. Ann's Parish Magazine," writing with respect to the present need for spending and sating wisely, says:— , " Shirkers and slackers and sparers of them- selves, are prolonging the war, increasing the dangers, delaying victory, postponing peace. Many scorn the words 'thrift' and 'economy:

They take them as meaning being miserly or stingy. A miser is-not thrifty, neither is being close-fisted economy. Thrift is an English word from thrive; to grow, get on, increase, to 'be in a healthy condition—thrift is the opposite to- harmful- waste. . Be thrifty, keep supplies in a healthy, sound condition. See to the ` overs ' that they arc not heedlessly thrown away. Do not spare some trouble to save even a little of the necessaries of life. Then again many are shy of ' economy ' and think ill of its practice. Face it . bravely, practise it regularly and economy will prove a friend. It is the father of thrift. It means good management not stingi- ness. It is acting on rule founded on knowledge, gained by • experience. Economy provides sufficient, not too lunch, or too little, just enough, then there is no waste and no cause to grumble. How are we to practise economy and be thrifty? Only general rules can be given. Each one must apply them to his or her own , ease. We can cut off unmcessaries. We can't . cut off the motor car. as we haven't one; still there are things we Can and ! should at'present do without, or use less. Make la:list of your week's spending. Let the items be tested by your yea] .need and your 'country's claim. Some will be lessened and others dis- appear in your next scrutiny. Try it and be good Spenders and good 'savers for fmr country's cause and true righteousness."

div.head: SAFETY OF THE ROAD.
div.p: THE SAFETY OF THE ROAD.

In proportion to the number of -cyclists acci- dents are most extraordinarily -rare. Probably there is no pastime so Safe. Certainly there is none that is safer. The few accidents that 419 occur are nearly always due entirely to care- lessness. This is not only true of cycling, but of all other i kinds of accidents which happen daily. At the root of all is lack of care on the part of someone.. Knowing this, it would be folly net to take warning. As cyclists it is impossible -foe us sometimes to avoid the fool motorist who goes at double the limit speed, or the errand boy who swings round corners at his best pace, or the pedestrian who meanders thoughtlessly from the footpath into the road- way. But by unceasing watchfulness and care we may avoid many disasters. It is very ofteu possible to "sense" what others are going to do, but naturally one cannot rely on this sixth sense too much. If every cyclist makes a point of riding at a fair and not excessive speed it will go a long way to making tlie public thor- oughfares less dangerous than they are at present. But the paramount point is that the machine 4hould be always under control. Never ride without being able to pull up at once.

div.head: CURE OF THE SQUEAK.
div.p: THE CURE OF THE SQUEAK.

:71-low often it happens that the driver of a motor car is almost distracted by unnecessary noises in his car, especially those of the squeaking variety. They are quite quaint, but exasperating in their illusiveness, and often give quite an unnecessary amount of trouble. The first thought, of .course, is oil, but not- withstanding the thorough lubrication of every portion of the mechanism under the .bonnet. the unpleasant noise Often continues. Exam- ination of the back axle gives no better result, and the tyro generally succeeds in meddling with every working part but the right one. Most often the trouble lies in the universal joint behind the gear-box, "which seems parti- cularly liable to evade or lose its grease, but, fortunately, a generous application of suitable lubricant usually brings the much-desired silent running. Another half-hearted squeak is often heard after the car has been in use for some months. This is often caused by the ends of the spring plated, which become dry and rub one another. However, this 'defect is very easy to locate, and by jacking up- the frame a little, thereby separating the leaves, a suffi- cient supply of grease can be rubbed round to last at least a year.

The Rev. J. D. Thompson (president of the conference) paid a visit to the ;.,r_xgh stre3t Primitive Methodist Church on Thursday, a lien he preached in the afternoon, and delivered a lecture on -" Christian Conscience and the War" in the evening. There were good attendances throughout the day, the evening service being presided over by Mr. J. Griffiths. •

-The lecturer asked who made this war? He had not the slightest hesitation in saying that 'Germany was responsible. If she had but lifted a finger this war would not have taken place. Where was Germany to-day? The Germany of to-day was a Germany of sheer barbaric mili- tarism. The Kaiser appealed to God. What God? The barbaric god Of the -Old Testament. "You call them women, do you?" asked a sadly war-damaged soldier, who, with a friend who had just donned khaki, was discussing the work being done by the Salvation Army StSters in the vast war area. "I call them angels, and so. they are!" he continued with emphasis. "All right, mate," responded his companion, "don't exert yourself! We're agreed; but, say, does your wife belong to—or is the Salvation Army your religion in civil life?" "Neither!" answered the other, "Listen, and I'll tell you why I'm their champion—not that they need one, you know." "I'd lost an arm and a leg, and was lying in hospital at Boulogne—almost dead—worrying myself worse about the missis and things, when one of the Army sisters came into the ward. I tell you, mate, the sight started the tears—it was such an echo of home. She had a little chat with all of us in our Ward, and when she came to me, straight, I blubbered like a kid. She knew I. was on the ' o.uted ' list, and seemed to be extra tender. She spoke about the missis, and asked me if I'd like to see her. " That did it. Lthought I was dead, but sid :` yes' and she wrote clown the address, smoothed the pillow, smiled again,--Prayed over me, and—she'd-gone!' . 'Well, next day the angel'came again, and she brought the .missis with her. "This. was .the -beginning.. of a turn for the- -better.
,• "After a day or so the missis went home, but the angel visited me regularly, wrote letters for me, and read letters sent to me.

" Then came the day when I was shipped for England, and she gave me—well, feel in that breast pocket, and you'll find a little Testament —that's what' she gave me. .Apart from my wounds its the only souvenir of the war I've got. "If you're here in half an hour from now see.another angel. This, one comes every week and chats with me. until I forget that I'm only half a. man." The work of these Sisters of Salvation has become one of the accepted things in the life of the common 'people. They flit hither and. thither in the course of their sacred ministry— here piloting a drunken .woman home, there washing neglected children and aiding the poor and feeble aged, somewhere -else smoothing the pillow of some otherwise forgotten', :worn-out child of shame—ready for any emergency, fear- ing nothing; caring ever for the world's un- lovables.

Some writer 'has termed these Salvation Sisters "Heroines in Blue." The title is excel- lent ; but the name "Sunny Sisters of Comfort " given to them by the men of our splendid fight- ing armies is still more apt and expressive.

War and Society. War has always influenced and often changed social Custonts. and usages: The introduction of pert wine, for instance, was dile to the constant war with France, that induced ministers to bring about a fiscal policy injurious to the enemy, but favourable to Portugal, then as now our faith- ful ally. The heavy- diet of the Georgian period was a necessary accompaniment to the heavier wines thus introduced. Before the outbreak of the present swar, Society was entirely given pp to pleasure, in its many and varied forms. London was a city of "cards and calls," but now the first are never left, and the second rarely made. Motors are given up, or lent to one or other of the many charitable organisations, and titled women ride in omnibuses as a matter of course. No doubt many of the "idle rich" have fallen back into the old ways, but as a. whole Society is now working as hard at nurs- ing, cooking, organising, &c., as ever it did at pleasure, and when peace comes the effect will be seen in the changed and improved social usages and manners. A new outlook on life must result from so much well-directed activity that has for its sole object the benefit of others.

CHEESE DISHES.

Macaroni and cheese.—For this dish the straight macaroni, which is -cheaper, answers just as well as the dearer twisted variety. Break it into pieces of a few inches in length, and put it into a pie-dish; two or three layers at the most is all that should be put into a rather deep 'pie-dish. Sprinkle a little salt over it, and well covcr it with milk or water—milk if procurable. Let it stand in a slow oven, covered with a plate, for about an hour, or until the macaroni is nicely softened and swollen. While it is in. the oven cut into thin flakes a good-sized piece of cheese, take the dish from the oven, and gently moves without breaking, the pieces of macaroni, so that the pieces of cheese may fall between, as well as on the top, as you scatter it in the dish. If all the milk has been ab- sorbed pour a little more over the mixture, add a little pepper and a few little pieces of butter, and bake for about three-quarters of an hour. If the oven is at all fierce cover the dish with a plate for the first half-hour, lest the top should become dry and chippy. 'Cheese Biscuits.—Two ounces of grated cheese, two ounces of -butter, two ounces of flour, a pinch, of cayenne pepper, and the yolk Of one egg. Rub the butter into the flour, mix in the finely grated cheese, add the cayenne, and moisten the ingredients with the yolk of the egg. Roll out the pastry until it is about an eighth. of an inch in thickness, stamp into rounds, and
baJye them in a moderate oven for fifteen min- ute. Serve the biscuits either hot or cold.

Cheese and tomato pie.—Take one pound of tomatoes, slice them and put a layer in a pie- dish. Then add a layer of grated cheese, and one of fine breadcrumbs, with peppqr and salt to taste. Continue these layers till the dish is full, the last layer must consist of cheese and bread- crumbs. Pour over half a pint of water, and put a few small pieces of butter on the top. Bake the pie in a moderate oven for abqut half an hour.

Cheese pasties.—Roll out some good short pastry, and divide it into pieces about six inches square. Then very lightly smear over one half of each square with mustard. 'Cut some cheese into thin slices and lay it over the mustard.' Fold the other half of the pastry over and pinch the edges together to prevent the cheese from running out during cooking. Bake the pasties in a moderate oven, and serve them very hot. These make a dainty luncheon or supper dish.

div.head: ASHI ON'S TONIC.
div.p: ASHI ON'S TONIC.
Laughter A Considerable Means
Of Health.
"LIT. AND PHIL." LECTURE

Having roamed the sciences of history, litera- ture, psychology, and physiology for theories and facts of laughter, Mr. H. M. Ashton Made members of the Literary and Philosophical Society laugh to their hearts' content on Mon- day evening, when he tabulated his discoveries. "Laughter is the right of man," he claimed forthwith. "The faculty of laughter is like all others; it. must find its own level, and if we re- tard its normal development we suffer. In- dulged in to a rational extent, it is a sign and cause of health. ' Laughter is one of the first in- stincts awakened in a child before it even learns to speak; and with what are babies amused? With everything and with nothing. With the light that lightens the day, with the fresh air whicli caresses them, with the smile which is bent upon them. They laugh spontaneously, just as they breathe. You know how. When the baby is passed round for inspection, and talked to and fondled, it crows with delight. It is its baby effort to show how pleased it is with everything you are doing for it. But if the • parents are morose and pessimistic and have gloomy faces, the very atmosphere becomes heavy and stifling, and It is the very young people of these parents who suffer the most. They pine for breatheable air. Heaven pre- serve us from those who are everlastingly giggling at nothing, and equally from those who go•through life without seeing any humour in it.
How to Amuse Children.

"Doctors class amongst the most ill the sad child, whose instinct of expansive joy has been crushed by physical suffering, or by the sadness of its surroundings. Learn before everything the art of amusing your child. Imitate the crow of the cockerel or roll on the carpet. Answer its thousand impossible questions, which are the echo of its endless dreams. Let it will your heard if you have one, your nose if not, and play at cuckoo in the corners. If you have made it laugh, it will want to do it again, and will run to you with its little arms open and cry, 'Again, daddy.' Says a writer for chil- dren One of my great means of seduction was this. I drew out my watch and looked at it very attentively. Then I would see my little chap stretch out his neck, strain his eyes, and advance with timid footsteps. Then I put my watch to my ear and smile like a man who is receiving a confidence. Before this wonder my babies cannot contain themselves, and shriek with joyous laughter.' The child grows and keeps for a long time this happy native gaiety. As a schoolboy he frequently manifests this gift of laughing without reason, solely for the physi- cal joy of it, and how ready he is to laugh at his schoolfellows' mistakes. Will you pardon me if I tell of a personal experience which illus- trates this 2 It was in my schoolboy days. The governor was taking a big class of us in English geography: • Newmarket was mentioned. 'Now, Ashton,' said .the governor. 'tell me what New- market is. famous for.' hadn't the faintest idea, and whispered to the boy next to me to tell me the right answer. Races' said he. I didn't quite catch what he said, but I answered 'Newmarket is famous for the manufacture of braces.' The class roared, but the governor gave me twenty bad marks, declaring I had made the mistake on purpose.
When Money Comes Before Life.

"A grown man, a prey to the thousand cares of daily life, and to the struggle for existence, is more difficult to cheer and brighten. The necessity to laugh as a means of relaxation, as a diversion, distraction, and expansion is not 'so apparent to him. The man whose sole object in life is to make money has no time for healthy, innocent laughter. His thoughts, waking or sleeping, are concentrated on the yellow god he worships. But the man who goes through life with the determination to do as much good and to get as much good as he can out of it, that man can _find every day some incident or acci- dent of his experience that will give him a happy, careless laugh. Every one of us in office, shop or warehouse, must remember some happening where a sense of humour saved the situation, so to speak. A few years ago, on a certain Saturday night at the busiest hour, a huge man, in liquor as we say, staggered into my pharmacy, followed by his wife. The latter pointed to a bleeding cut on the man's head, and asked me to plaster it up. I did my best, though naturally feeling annoyed. Just as he was staggering out, he pulled off the plaster, and holding it up to me said •' Give it another lick, mister, it ain't sticking!' I simply had to laugh then. _ _

div.head: Bald Elisha.
div.p: Bald Elisha.

"The Bible gives us the early history of the world," he Went on, "but we could hardly ex- pect it would deal with the lighter side of life. There seems to have been very little encourage- ment given to people with a. sense of humour. In fact, the only -atteitipt at levity recorded in the Old Testament history—which I can call to mind—seems to have met with the most disastrous results. I refer. to tlie.in'u .f 'be hap v 1 joyous children who came out and laughed at Elisha, the prophet, and -mocked him for his lack of hirsute adornment—and mind you, I am in "sympathy, with Elisha to 'a certain extent. —(laughter)—but I have my doubts as to the justice of their punishment. .. . It was very discouraging and must have put a check on humour in that neighbourhood for many genera- tions. And talking of bears reminds me of a teacher who was giving a lesson on 'The Bear,' and -speaking of his thick, warm coat, said And can the bear take oK his coat like you can?'
"'No, teacher,' came the reply. "'Why cannot the bear take off his coat?' " ' Please, teacher, because God only knows where the buttons are!'

" And there is a:mention of Elijah laughing at the prophets of Baal in their vain attempts to light the fire on the altar by praying to their false gods. Ecclesiastes, the preacher, seems to have had a very poor opinion of laugh- ter as an asset in the business of life. He says-: 'Sorrow is better than-laughter, for by sadness of the countenance the heart is made better," and, again, I said of laughter it is mad, of mirth what doeth it?' Deadly Jokes.

• "In fact we find very little mention of laughter in the ancient histories of the world, and it is not to be wondered at, for the his- torian in compiling his work cannot be ex- pected to record the occasions when this or that great personage laughed. It may be that the general tenor of humour in those days was of too brutal and coarse a nature to be per- petuated on papyrus. Amongst the Romans the idea of fun and humour seemed to partake a great deal of the nature of savagery. To see slaves and martyrs mangled, torn and eaten was to them a great joke. . . . 'Shakespeare created some very humorous characters in his •plays, although he put his strength into tragedy and played with comedy. There are scenes and characters in Shakes..

peare which equal in wit anedrollery any- thing on record. Falstaff is the leviathan of all the creations of the author's comic genius, and tumbles about his unwieldly bulk in an ocean ,of wit and humour. But in general it will be found that even in the very -best of these the spirit. of humanity and the fancy of the poet greatly' prevail over the mere wit and satire, and we sympathise with his characters oftener than we laugh at them. His ridicule wants the' sting of ill-nature. Falstaff himself is so great a joke rather from his being so huge a mass of enjoyment than of absurdity. Touchstone again is a shrewd, biting fellow, a lively wag, but what are his gibing sentences and his chopped logic to the fine moralising veiny- of the fantastic Jacques, stretched beneath the shade of melancholy boughs? Nothing. I al- ways regard Dogberry as one of the greatest laughter-creating characters of Shakespeare His misplacement of words in the most serious manner, or what may be termed his malapro- pism's, are most droll."
Stories I n Point.

Having illustrated his Shakespearean conten— tions by making quotations, Mr. Ashton told. stories demonstrating various causes of laughter, such as exaggeration and absurd answers peopl are apt to give to absurd questions. For in- stance, he recalled, the other day- a man fell through a coal-hole, sprained his ankle, and remained a prisoner for five and twenty minutes He called for help in vain. It was a quiet street, and nobody patronised it. Meanwhile the pain increased and the unfortunate way- farer nearly fainted. He opened his eyes to find an old gentleman regarding him. "Dear me," said the kind-hearted pedestrian, putting on his pincenez, "Have you fallen through that coal-hole?" "Not at all," replied the man winningly. "As you seem interested in the matter I will tell you what happened. I chanced to be here and they built the pavement round me!" A Lecturer's High Dive.

"And the glass of water you have placed for me reminds me of another story," continued Mr, Ashton. "A lecturer asked for a glass of water and he was asked if he wanted it to drink. 'Oh, no,' he said. In the course of my lecture I take a high dive!'" Taken in proper doses, Mr. Ashton concluded, laughter was hygienic. It was an aid to better living, and was one of the elenients of the good state of the body. Acting as a kind of valve, it delivered us from an excess of energy, and enabled us to expend an overflow of nervous electricity or latent force. Thanks to laughter, respiration became more active, the warmth of the body increased and digestion was materially improved. Laughter was ecnecially of moment to our moral hygiene. When we had laughed with a good heart did we not feel more kindly disposed, more ready with sympathy and kind deeds?
Ilor his lecture Mr. Ashton was heartily thanked, those concerned in the Society's ex- nression being the President (the Rev. A. V. Pigot), Mr. A. J. Jolley, Mr. J. H. Smethurst and Dr. Manson.

div.head: PROTECTIONISTS.
div.p: PROTECTIONISTS.

Protection, like National Service has broken out badly: No. sooner had the war come upon us than the advocates of compul- sory military service, seeking to-further their own desires by means of national calamity, shrieked for compulsion. That demand was steadily resisted, and the voluntary system was not .only saved but magnificently justi- fied itself by giving the country 6,000,000 free men to fight its battles. The dregs are i to be collected in by force, it s true, but Eng- land stands loyal as ever to the voluntary system. Now it is' the turn of the Protection- ist. He is trying to force down our throats his old-time nostrum while our hatred of Ger- man methods is at white.heat. The Manches- ter Chamber of Commerce has been induced to incline to the reactionary side. But the time for settling a trade policy will surely. be after the war, when conditions are known and when common-sense and ascertained interest will prevail, rather than the haphazard argu- ment of the daily student. of war news. The spirit in which this serious question, that alleets vitally nearly all, if not all, our indus- trial life is approached, is fairly well sh,..vsn in the following letter we have receive.; 1:4.m Mr. C. 'E. Cowper, of Lymm, and of the firm of C: Cowper and Co., .Manchester

Free Trade we have never had, as yet; all on one side for the foreigner. Let us do all we can for our' own Colonies who have supported us so nobly in this war. Tax the German goods in future anil enable us to pay higher wages to our own people. Thank God there is a stir in the Man- chester Chamber of Commerce at last. I was a member for a while, but the place was packed with foreigners, mostly Germans, that I requested Mr. Speakman to take my name off as a subscriber. The lot there do not represenT manufac- turers wto employ labour, but mostly foreign firms who live on those that keep stocks.

We are not able to accept Mr. Cowper's assertions as conclusive arguments. True W 9 shall have to consider most carefully our reit.- tions for the future with the fiends who tall themselves Germans; but we must cons;der the question in a judicial spirit and make sure that we do not bite off our nose to s?ite our face. At any rate, we shall bew:t..f) of those who, urging us to change, take for their preamble the sentence, as Mr. Cowper c.oes, Free Trade we have never had, as yqt; ril one side for the foreigner." For our part we would prefer to respect the political truce and keep away from politics altogether till the war has been won. All our energies are claimed by that one task.

His habit came out in this way. He was detailing how he was persuaded to attend that. function. It was on a Sunday morning and, Miss Forshaw rang him up on the telephone while he WAS in retirement, and would not go away until he spoke to her and consented to come.
I like the idea of Cafe Chantant. It Made one long for more of these agreeable functions. To sit at a tea table while music is discoursed savours pleasantly of Arcadia—or Lyon's.

div.head: SHIP CANAL PAYS!
div.p: SHIP CANAL PAYS!
A YEAR OF ACTIVE SER,VICE.

I We learn from a 'letter, which Colonel Fairclough has sent to the Town Clerk, that last Saturday was the first anniversary of the landing of the Warrington Territorials on French soil. It has been an eventful and anxious twelve months for the town, for few have been the families that have not had at least one member upholding the honour of country amid unprecedented dangers, even as dangers go on the battlefield. The foe we are now meeting does not know what honour means, and the methods he has adopted have cast additional burdens upon those who have gone forth, to meet him. Our local men have ' joined wholeheartedly in the work of stem- ming the Hun onslaught on humanity; they have shared the glories of charging in. the front rank, and' they will add lustre to the standard of the regiment to which they be- long, a regiment that has a 'record second to none in the great accumulation of names that the building of our Empire has called' into being. We refer .specially to the Territorials in this manner, because they are peculiarly representative of the town and neighbourhood and are a collective body to whom Ive can specifically and conveniently refer. But, of course, they do but represent a proportion of the many sons who, in •every section of' the forces, on land and sea and 'in the air, repre- sent Warrington; . which has, despite a few. slanderers, done its work nobly and well, .and will be among the last to cry "Hold, enough!" Our congratulations, then, to Colonel TaireloUgh and his men upon having borne the brunt of warfare so well for a whole year. May the second anniversary of that fateful sailing and landing, when many said " Good-bye ' to the dear old country for ever," see peace well established, the Hun having in the meantime been rendered help- less for mischief for all time to come.

div.head: OUR ROTTEN BOROUGH.
div.p: OUR ROTTEN BOROUGH.

When we recall all these things that have been done in the name of the town we wonder how it comes to be possible that a person who has spent most of his time inventing reasons why he should not help, can allow himself, or be allowed in the presence of. a body who are supposed to represent the working men of Warrington, to speaz of Warrington as "Your Rotten Borough." The Trades Coun- cil, as at present constituted, is condemned. It will be noticed with pleasure by all right- -thinking men that the Engineers and the Dock Labourers and Riverside Workers have joined others and seceded from the Trades Council. That Council, by allowing to pass unchallenged the statement that their borough was rotten, condemn themselves as clearly as did their hostility to the Army, their neutrality to recruiting, their churlish conduct when asked to lissist in the thrift movement, and their deliberate attempt to slander 10,000 working men of Warrington when they claimed to say, in their behalf, • hat the Government and Lord Kitchener were not to be supported in a 'final effort to win the war. We look with confidence to .the remaining unions to take such action as will finally relieve the town of the stigma that, in spite of its grand record, has been cast upon it. Again we ask, as at the outset, "For whom do the Trades Council speak?"— whether it be with regard to military matters or the rottenness-of the borough.

' Had we been dealing with anybody but Mr. Chas. Dukes, the secretary of the modern Trades Council, we should have expected him to apologise for this crude expression. But calmer moments, it seems, have not brought about repentance; the policy is studied and deliberate, and the reply of all genuine -workers must be studied and deliberate, too. The Dock Labourers have indicated the proper method of procedure.. They have de- cided .to ask other societies to take joint action in forming "a Trades Council for purely trade union purposes." That puts the matter into practical, concrete shape, and we hope the unions will get to work upon those lines forthwith. As soon as the war is over many questions will have to be considered and the trade union privileges, which have been necessarily impinged upon, will have to be re-instituted, as per Mr. Asquith's prom- ise. The men to join in this. work will not be, the men who have been sulking while the nation has been securing its larger privileges of life and freedom. As-Mr. Baker -told the Wiredrawers, there is good work to be done, and we shall want good trusty men to do it. Therefore, let the unions get to business by putting in a good foundation betimes. Those who dub as rotten Warrington, that has given so lavishly of its blood and thought and ser- vice, will not be safe guides to put us on the right pith. Let us have done, then, with the Trades and Labour Council—as at present constituted.

div.head: PASSING GENERATION.
div.p: A PASSING GENERATION.
Alderman Smethurst One Of Remaining Pioneers.

The making of the Ship Canal was the work of one generation; the fruits, so far as divi- dends are concerned, will be reaped by another, although in the meantime the North of Eng- land has benefited enormously by being pro- ,vided with an inland port. In the fight for the Bill in the.early 'eighties. Warrington, where there was to have been an intermediate dock, fought strenuously for Man- chester, and, of course, against Liverpool. We had a great hand in getting the powers, and then we did our share towards finding the colossal sum of money that was necessary to construct the great waterway. Alderman Smethurst, who was one of the Warrington committee that worked for the Canal, and who backed up his belief in the need for the undertaking and faith in its ulti- mate success by investing largely in its funds, was very elated last Saturday morning when seen by an " Examiner " representative on the subject. div.head: Complex Leather Trade Conditions.
div.p: Complex Leather Trade Conditions.

Trade continues to run very actively upon all classes of leather, the demand being more than equal to all produced. Government de- mands are not very heavy just now, and I believe the much-talked-of Russian order is still "in the air," and by jest/so much is the sitqa- tion at present relieved. With the quick call- ing up of the Derby groups, however, Army re- quirements are likely to grow quickly, and that the home trade has this in mind is shorn by the avidity with which even the smallest par- cels are being taken up as opportunity affords. Prices are moving stoadily upwards; the move- ment, at first confined to bends, is now general, and it is almost an impossibility to buy any- thing on old terms; to take time to consider in -many cases is to miss the goods, as in the mean- timb another buyer has come along and taken them. It is also difficult to obtain offers for for- ward delivery, as, for reasons easily under. stood, most tanners will sell only stock which is on the floor, and the most tempting offers usually fail to move them from this position. Taken altogether, the situation is very complex and extraordinarily difficult for all concerned, and apparently the only safe course for both seller-and buyer is just to deal with trade on a day-to-day, basin.

div.head: MR. BURTON RESIGNS.
div.p: MR. BURTON RESIGNS.

The meeting opened with a sad note. Alder- man T. Burton, who has been chairman of the committee for many years and has taken an active interest in its welfare since its earliest days, has for the last twelve months been too ill to attend its meetings. He has asked to be allowed to resign several times, but the corn- mittee have persuaded him to remain at their head. However, on Wednesday Mr. Hampson read the following decisive letter:—
• "19, Stafford-road, Warrington, January 27th, 1916. Working Men's Committee, Warrington Infirmary.

" Gentlemen,—l feel that the time has now come when I should resign from the committee. It is no easy matter to do so after being con- nected with it so many years, but I feel it is better to do it now than at the annual meeting later on: I should like to tender t4y thanks to Mr. Walker and Mr. Ilanipson and all the mem- bers of the committee for the admirable way they have carried on the work during the year. I hope the year's labour of the committee will be crowned with financial success. "Yours sincerely, " MOB. BURTON."

Mr. Wadsworth suggested that they might still keep Alderman Burton as the nominal head of the committee; but Mr. Hampson said the Chairman had quite made up his mind. It was therefore decided, on the proposition of Mr. G. E. Knott (Rylands Bros.) that the resignation be accepted with regret, and that Mr. George Walker be nominated for the chair- manship at the annual meeting.

Daintith Incident.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—The reason "Shint " Daintith will not be included in our team to-morrow is owing to an.objection raised by the Warrington Rugby F.C., who -refuse to grant tile 'necessary permit to allow him to play for us. Daintith has now played two matches for us and is very anxious to continue with the Town team during the absence of the Rugby game in Warrington. The attitude taken by the Warrington Rugby Club is, to say the least of it, very paltry, especially at this time, when players do not receive any remuneration for services rendered. _

Warrington have, of course, granted a permit to Daintith to play for the Runcorn N.U. Club, but at what inconvenience to the player? The Warrington Town Club has, so far, met with success; in fact, much more than the local Rugby Club appreciate; hence the objec- tion.

The population of Warrington is nearly 80,000 and surely there is room for Aociation as well as Rugby. I may say that Daintith is very much butt at the attitude taken up by the Rugby Club, thus debarring him from playing with a team so near at hand, with less inconvenience than playing out of tha town.—Yours, &c.„
P. PEACOCK, Jun.

Palestine Nineteen Centuries Ago. Commencing a series of lectures on "Pales- tine in the Apostolic Age," Mr. A. -Mounfield, in Friars' Green Schoolroom, gave an informa- tive sketch of the history which preceded the New Testament era. After the death of Alexander the Great, his kingdom was divided amongst his Generals, and Syria and Palestine passed to one of them, name Antiochus. This Emperor endeavoured to suppress the Jewish religion and turned their Temple into a heathen temple. After a long and bitter struggle the people succeeded and for a time followed their own religious usages. But in- ternal differences brought weakness, and when Rome gained ascendency, Pompey the tato. us General, took possession of Palestine. The stirring and 'terrible events of the three cen- turies before the Christian era left their mark upon the people and led to the formation of many sects. The common people looked earn- estly for a deliverer and anticipated that the Messiah, promised in Old Testament writings, would be a military leader, who would crush their oppressors and give them a leading place among the nations. A description of the Jewish sects, religion and usages in the days oY the Apostles would form the subject of the lectures which were to follow. We are very sorry indeed, says the "Sheffield Daily Telegraph," to hear that the Rev. J. F. Matthews is concluding his ministry at the Glossop-road Baptist Church. div.head: WEAR AND TEAR OF THE MUM
div.p: THE WEAR AND TEAR OF THE MUM
The Need For Courage And For Sympathy.
BY ,C. E. PARKER.

During the continuance of the war we are steadily accumulating a heavy liability, the result of wear and tear, which will have to be met in the future. Only absolutely necessary repairs are being executed, and much will have to be undertaken at the end of the war to bring the mechanical adjunctfeto labour up to their normal efficiency. Machine railways, power plants, steamships, are all being worn down, and the cost of repairs and replacement will, be heavy. • But it is not of the wear and tear of mechanical contrivance's that I wish to speak, but of the wear and tear of the human mechanism. This although less tangible, is the,more real and important. Our victory or defeat is dependent upon the toughness the endurance of the fibre of our national spirit, and to the extent we can repair the wear and tear of body and mind. Contention Over Minor Matters.

AB a nation we have done well—we might have done better. We cannot be blind to the fact that there are a number of our people who are not doing all they can. These have not yet appreciated the fact that at this hour the future of the world is at stake that momentous issues tremble in the balance. Hence minor issues, indiVidual and class in- terests (important it may be in ordinary times, but insignificant in view of the great stake involved) arc emphasised and contended for as if these were the chief things and the outcome of this conflict of secondary'import- ence. This attitude is not confined to any particular class or locality. We find it in high places as well as in low, in Parliament, and especially in a section of the Press. Probably the Press, or rather a portion of it, has been the worst offender, and one would think that the criticisms indulged in were designed for the sole purpose of popularising the papers rather than of strengthening the spirit of the nation. This does not imply that we should depreciate legitimate criticism. This is valuable to maintain efficiency, but much of the Press criticism shows little know- ledge, discrimination or fairness, and only tends to weaken the unity of the nation, and waste the force and discourage the spirit of its rulers.

In this time of trial nothing is more marked than the inequality of the sacrifice demanded. Some have sacrificed, and are sacrificing their best. Many have parted with husbands and sons who have gone to the Front, the danger zone. They have said farewell to these in our undemonstrative English way, fearful less their sorrow should cloud the spirit of the lad who has gone off with high hopes and brave determination worthily to play his part in the titanic struggle: And these parents, wives, and lovers have gone wearily home feeling much b.t.lt saying little, realising that the best of their heart and life has gone with the, absent one. On the other hand others because of their circumstances, have suffered little or nothing in person, family, or estate. Upon the latter especially, though not alone on such, falls the obligation to take upon .themselves, an far as it is possible, some of the burden of those who have laid upon them more than they can bare. The German Burden.

Since the war began nothing has come to light that has given us reason to doubt that we , were .wrong when we entered this fight. After eighteen months, in winch we have had an opportunity to study the causes which plunged Europe into the welter of war, we are now more disposed even than at the begin- ning to agree with Mr. Asquith when he said; 'Sooner than be a silent witness—which means in effect an accomplice—to this tragic triumph of force over law and brutality over freedom' I would see this country blotted out from the pages of history." We have the faith to believe that right will be triumphant in the end, but the triumph may be long de- layed if we do not all throw our whole strength into the struggle. We have every reason for encouragement. Even the territorial tri- umphs of Germany are a prelude and a promise of her ultimate defeat, because she has paid too big a price for these successes. The her- culean efforts made by our foes to extend their conquest of territory have worn their strength, wasted their resources' without yielding an adequate advantage. The same strain, the effect of which we want to guard against at home has told, and is telling, upon the spirit of Germany to a greater degree than upon ourselves. Her people are war- worn and the strain, is telling with accumulat- ing effect. But the end is not yet; it would be folly to rely upon an early exhaustion. German military power is still strong, and will fight to the death, because it has staked its all upon this issue. The system of mili- taryism slavery has deceived, misled and cowed the mind and the spirit of German democracy, and establisheid an ascendency over the whole people. They. have, as a whole, accepted the fiction of the 'danger of the Fatherland, and the strongest of national virtues, that of patriotism, has been evoked. But time is on our side, the reserves of the Allies in men and resources are far greater than those of Germany and his Allies. Sacrifice and Selfishness.

It only requires a steady continuation of our determination to conquer, to sacrifice everything to the one end, that of ensuring a final and complete victory. We must 'stick it" to a finish, and everyone must do his part. Of those who are at the Front, or in training, we have no fear. It is the selfish, the croakers, the fearful and the weary at home that cause most concern. Of these, the selfish are the worst, the men who are holding back their part of the price, seeking to get all they can out of this war for themselves, wasting in drink or other luxuries the wealth the nation so sorely needs, refusing to respond in the many calls for help and for sacrifice. This selfishness looks ugly when we set it side by side with the splendours of unselfishness which others are manifesting. In this war there have been evidences in the conduct of many of a real dethronement, an eviction of self which before the war, perhaps unconsciously, governed the life. To the fearful and weary we must afford strength, consolation and help. These states of mind result from a variety of causes. They are the natural results of the industrial, social and family upheavals due to the war. A considerable portion of our people have had their means of livelihood .diminished either by reduced earnings or in- creased prices, in spine cases by both, exces- sive work beyond their powers has been thrown upon others. Grief, anxiety, and diminished necessities naturally eat into the courage of those who are thus burdened. These are producing a condition of strain and ex- haustion amongst many of our people, and as the war goes on their numbers will increase. A Patriotic Service.

There is no more useful, no more patriotic work for those who are able than to seek out such, and to help them to bear the loads that are becoming too heayy. Let everyone seek to repair, to save the human wear and 'tear, and let the beginning be made at his own door. We must discountenance all that creates disunion, strengthen and sustain the weak and weary, comfort the anxious and the bereaved. Everyone must do his best to hearten the courage and tauten the tenacity of the nation. " Stick it, Dorsets t" cried a dying officer in Flanders last autumn, and this must be our motto in the months to come. The supreme test has not yet come to our people, the wear and tear will become greater, and those of us who are left at home must guard again ct t.b.L wcar and teat in ourselves and others.,

SERGEANT STANLEY PARTRIDGE.
Warrington Cricketer Hit By Rifle Grenade.

Sergeant Stanley Partridge, a gentleman who has been prominently before the eyes of the Warrington public, has been wounded in the head and right arm by a rifle grenade while engaged in a raid with a bombing party. The incident occurred on the sth inst., while he was serving with the 18th Battalion 2nd City King's (Liverpool) Regiment, a. "Pals" Battalion, which includes many professional gentlemen from Warrington. The news was conveyed to his parents, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Partridge, of the Imperial Hotel, Bewsey-road, through a letter sent by Corporal •Harry •Rushworth to his father, Mr. J. A. Rushworth, licenses of the Horse and Jockey Hotel, Winwick-road. The letter read:

"Stanley Partridge was wounded last, Satur- day afternoon (February sth), but I am glad to say it was only slight. I was present when the doctors dressed his wounds, and he appeared to be all right. The worst of it is you never know how these wounds turn out. It was a rifle grenade that caught him. One piece hit him on the right arm, above the elbow, and another caught his head, but only bruised it. div.head: But Sergeant Cheerfully Drills
div.p: But Sergeant Cheerfully Drills
Recruits.
REMARKABLE EXPERIENCE.

Despite the presence a a bullet within an ace of his, heart, Sergeant John Barr, well-known as a cornet player in Warrington, stands as up- right as any. instructtr, and now takes pleasure in drilling recruits at Rhyl. His experience furnishes the most remarkable instance of the war, so far as Warrington is con- cerned.

He was in Gallipoli in November, when a sniper shot him. The bullet entered his right breast and then rested close to his heart, be- tween the second and third ribs. It is there now. Hei carried it to England via Malta, and has been examined several Hines by doctors, who advise that it should remain in residence
SERGEANT JOHN BARE. Wounded.
until it troubles him. For it is a remarkable fact that he suffers no pain, has no physical cognisance of its presence, and his temperament is, if anything, more cheerful and urbane than ever.

That the bullet is there, however, there is no doubt. One day while standing in his pyjamas in hospital the doctors took an X-rays photo- graph and the bullet, pointing directly at his heart, was clearly shown. He has an enlarge- ment framed and hanging up in the parlour of his house, 20, Scott-street, off Battersby-lane. The Sergeant has been in/ England several weeks now. He has been before a medical board, who have passed him for home service. Hating concluded a holiday in Warrington, he has been dispatched to a centre to train recruits for the Front.

div.head: Still Plays The Cornet.
div.p: Still Plays The Cornet.

What adds interest to his case is that he is able to play his cornet in as sound a manner as hitherto. Every night of the fortnight he spent at home he practised on this instrument and, once, when asked whether he was not afraid of the bullet being shifted by the pressure, he re- plied, "Playing strengthens my chest." Having been sQlo cornet player in Down's Military and Orchestral Band, it was natural that while he was in this part of the country he should engage in practice with them. This he did last week, and his.old friends manifested their delight in seeing him again. Sergeant Barr has been connected with many bands: He has had the distinction of being Drum-Major for his regiment, the King's Own Royal Lancasters; played in Crosfield's Band when they won the cup at the Crystal Palace; and, in addition, has been a member of the C.L.C., the Pioneer, and the Buffaloes Bands. Excepting for five years, when be worked for the Cheshire Lines Railway Co. and the Man- chester Ship Canal Co., he has been almost con- tinuously devoted to soldiering since his youth. He served in the Royal Lancaster Regiment for many years, going to several of our colonial possessions with them, in addition to being stationed at HonWKong. Went Through South African War.

He served in South Africa throughout the war there, and has both the Queen's' and King's medals. The former has two bars on—Laing's Nek and Transvaal—the latter three—Relief of Ladysmith, Orange Free States and Tugela Heights. •

The recently-appointed local tribunal under the Military Service Act has not yet com- menced its sittings. It will be remembered that at a special meeting of the Council held last week Messrs. div.head: WARNING TO THE UNATTESTED.
div.p: WARNING TO THE UNATTESTED.

The War Office announce that every unmar- ried man to whom the Military Service Act applies must, if he desires exemption, make an application before March 2nd to the local tribunal.
