div.head: BULLIES AT HOME!
div.p: BULLIES AT HOME!
Treatment For Those Who Invent
Reasons For Shirking.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."
Kingsley, Hill Chile, 17th February, 1916.

Sir,—There are some men in our midst who openly boast that they "have not attested, will not attest, and nobody shall, make them attest." One of the speakers at the recent meeting of the Wiredrawers' -Union stated that, in his opinion, any man who shirked his duty in our country's great hourcof need "ought to be put against the wall and shot: Men who are pre- pared to ,take all the benefits of freedom and security that our country affords and at the same time shamefully boast of their determina- tion to shoulder no responsibility, are worse than useless—they are a distinct menace to the security of. the State and should be treated accordingly. I send you herewith an extract from a recent letter received from the' Dardanelles, which, while it will have no effect on the type of indi- vidual to whom I have already referred, will at least prove that the rising generation has in- herited all the nobler characteristics of our race; and to those who, like myself, are too far advanced in years to render physical service (but who can help to bear some of the burdens which are incidental to the present colossal struggle) it gives ample ground for absolute confidence that the sacrifices so freely made by our loved ones will not have been in vain, for out of all this .welter of sorrow and bloodshed, a new England and a new Empire will be born, in which her people, purified, strengthened and disciplined, will realise that exaltation of pur- pose and character which the righteousness of our present cause will produce. Yours, de., H. ROBERTS.
Extract from the letter of a Staff Officer in he Dardanelles, on the question of compulsion:
" Jan:nary, 1916. "I expect to hear soon that compulsion has at Ast been declared, and a good job too.. .

None of our big men here want compulsion for its own sake But if the slackrirs woi't come forward quick enough by the so-called ' voluntary ' efforts which have been made, then compulsion it must be! "If the women of England could see the sights which we have seen daily and notice the hardships borne and the pluck and bravery dis- played by British lads out here, many of whom were at school when the war broke out, they would hound the men out. The day before we evacuated Helles, the Turks gave us hell, with every gun they had on the Peninsula going for all it was worth for six hours without ceasing, and at the end of that, British lads were tightly grasping their rifles, ready for the Turks' ex- pected attack, and some even standing on the top of the parapet, shouting to the Turk and inviting him to come out! Trenches broken everywhere—men buried, leis, arms and heads lying about, and still these lads thought only of the enemy in front.

"Don't you think there is something rotten in the State when England permits her boys to do the fighting for these bullies at home?.—who seem to be good at talking and inventing reasons why they should not fight! "I was in the evacuation of Suvia and Relies. After evacuating Suvla, we thought to have a well-earned rest, but after four days' peace, our .division was sent to Relies, only, as it turned out, to carry out the evacuation there. How- ever, I would not have inissed the latter on any account. lam not allowed to say how the trick was done, but it is the first time in history that a force has been withdrawn from close contact with the enemy without heavy loss in life and stores. They were very interesting and anxious times, but I am glad they are over and we are to have a res."

RAGTIME AND THE TANGO.

Whe6 the curtain curled up in the great concert hall at the Lord Derby Military Hos- pital, Winwick, on Tuesday evening, hundreds of hands were clapped with enthusiasm at'the novel appearance of a baker's-dozen of con- valescents forming a picturesque and gay half- circle on the stage. They were the cream of the musical and acting talent in the hospital, and were about to begin to 'display their vocal and histrionic wares. The beautiful and commodious hall was crowded. Just behind Major ;Nash (an excel- lent conductor) sat the doctors, then scores of nurses, tens of limbless lads in mobile beds and perambulating chairs, and a great back- ground of soldiers masse4 in close quarter- column order. A frame of nurses standing round ready to attend to expressed needs com- pleted the human picture. It was a gala night. Many are the concerts which have been held here, but almost without hesitation one can say that this was the most pleasing. div.head: TRAGEDY OF ARMENIA.
div.p: THE TRAGEDY OF ARMENIA.

shock of horror and irbdignation has pulsated through all civilised communities at the ruthless Wing of her Christian subjects .by Turkey. It was recently estimated by Lord Bryce that 800,000 Armenians had been cruelly done to death, while only a week or two ago the news reached him that 1,500 had been forced to abandon the shelter of the mountains, and had been massacred by their persecutors. One feels stunned and helpless in the face, of this monstrous' wrong, and for these victims there is nothing to be done; they are in their Father's hands, and at rest for ever. , But the 'survivors claim our pity and. help. Nearly a quarter of a million—by Lord Bryce's estimate e4.ca.ped into the Caucasus, destitute and staring; many fell by the way, others reached their destination, only to 'die of disease and exhaustion. America has sent a Relief. Commission to aid these refugees in the Caucasus; two Members of the 'Commission are well-known to us, as for many years they have been almoners of our funds in Turkey, and they are entirely devoted to the interests of the poor people among whom they'have lived for so long. At Port Said there are over. 1,000 refugees who were rescued in a remarkable manner from the Syrian mountains.: These people are living in tents provided by the British authorities, but it is necessary that they should become self-sup- porting, and our chief aim in helping them is to provide materials for starting industrial work among them, and helpers to organise the work. To this end we have sent out a lady of great experience, formerly a worker in Syria, and we hope that two other workers will shortly follow her, sent out under our auspices to give the assistance so greatly needed. But for even partial help for all these thousands of unhappy people money is needed and more and more money ! In the Caucasus winter accommodation is required, fuel in large quantities is needed. Warm clothing and an ample supply of food- stuffs, medicines, medical appliances and dis- infectants are of paramount necessity, and although these cannot be sent to the Caucasus until the Port of Archangel reopens about the middle of April, funds will, enable us to prepare them. We have recently forwarded £l,OOO to rrumia, for the help of the Armenians and Tsiestorians there, and we plead for further adequate assistance, to keep alive this remnant of a nation. We know the many demands on the charitable at this time—demands which must be heeded, but this, surely, is as urgent as any can be! Which among the nations has suffered as this nation has suffered? The majority of the refugees comiist of women and children—little tender things, many of whom are suffering from bronchitis, and other ills brought about by want and exposure. We ask all who can to help relieve this tragedy of sorrow—to make some sacrifice for these men, women and children of grief, misery- ane. bereavement.
I am, Sir,
Yours faithfully, MARY HICKSON, Hon. Sec. Friends of Armenia.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS AND DRINKING FACILITIES.
div.p: DRUNKENNESS AND DRINKING FACILITIES.

Sir,—The teetotalist policy of ti'.3eu:.•,..s. mine- tion and shorter hours stands or falls on the assumption that drunkenness varies in direct ratio with facilities. for obtaining drink, that is to say that the greater the facilities, the greater the drunkenness; the less the facilities the less the drunkenness.
This theory received a nasty knock in the recent annual report of the Wigan Chkf Con- stable, which contains a table giving drunken- ness figures for 17 large Lancashire and Cheshire towns for 1915.

Let us take three of these towns and compare them with another Once, and we shall expect (on the teetotalist theory) to find the mass, of drunkt.nness coinciding, to some extent at events, 'with the number of licensed houses, but do we?
Accrington, Bolton and Bacnp (with a total population of 248,258 in 1911) have last year 702 licences and 331 arrests for drunkenness.
Birkenhead, Bootle and Warrington (popula- tion 1911, 272,836) had 493 licences and 1,947 arrests for drunkenness.

Three towns have 702 licences and only 331 drunks; the other three with only 493 licences have 1,947 drunks! For every hundred licences in the first three towns there were only 47.1 arrests; in the other three we find 391.9.
How can teetotalers and rOstrictionists explain these figures, which are just the opposite of what they should be if there is any truth in their theory?
J. E. SIMPSON
February 12th, 1916.

div.head: FARM FIRE.
div.p: FARM FIRE.
Irish Farm Labourers Charged With
Arson
AND DISCHARGED.
£250 worth of hay and wheat, and a ,hayshed valued at £l2O were destroyed by fire on Sunday night at Mr. Harry Warburton's, Old Hall Farm, Thelwall.

The police fearing that arson had been com- mitted, arrested two Irish farm labourers who were alleged to have been seen hurrying away from the farm about the time the cereals began to blaze, and on Monday they were charged at an Occasional Court, being remanded until Wed- nesday, when they were dismissed. The men were Thomas Duggan, of Croutchley Farm, Lymm, and Michael Higgins, of Perkins' Farm, High Legh, and they pleaded not guilty to a charge on suspicion of maliciously setting on , fire a hayshed containing 10 tons of hay value £5O, 25 tons of unthreshed oats value £9O, and ty stack of unthreshed wheat valut: £6O, the property of Mr. H. Warburton; they also pleaded not guilty to a charge of setting on fire the hayshed, the property of Mr. Henry Stanton. It was stated that Mr. Stanton was Mr. War- burton's landlord and, therefore, owned the shed. Arthur Ellis Brooks, of Morley Farm, Thel- wall, said that at 9.15 on Sunday night, when he walked in the direction of Lymm, he neither saw a fire nor anyone about, but a few minutes later, when he returned, he saw a blaze which made him run towards the farm. As he did so he saw the two prisoners about 250 yards away from the farm. They were going "pretty sharp" at a fast walk, not quite a run. Ile did not stop tlwm and ask them to go back to the farm because they were under the influence of drink. He could tell they were Irishmen from their talk. On receiving information, Sergeant Davies arrested the men, who immediately denied that they had been near the farm, or even knew of its whereabouts.

div.head: " Innocent as a Child."
div.p: " Innocent as a Child."
Duggan: I am charged wrong. I am as inno- cent as a child.

Higgins: I never went there. Mn! Warburton stated that Duggan worked for him three or four years ago, and he had no bother with him. The stack was ten or twelve Yards away from the road, and he did not think anyone smoking could have thrown a match on it when walking by. He would have to go through the gate to do so. n The magistrates retired to consider their e- cesion and, on returning, Mr. Alfred Watkin (the chairman) said the magistrates were of opinion that the police were justified in bring- ing the case for investigation, as there were undoubtedly suspicious points, but the magis- trates did not think a jury would ,convict. There was not sufficient evidence for the case to go to Assizes
Higgins: I should think not. Mr. Watkin: And, therefore, the prisoners will be dismissed.
QUELLING THE FLAMES.

When the. fire was discovered by Mr. Brooks, he immediately proceeded to the farm and dis- turbed Mr. Warburton, who had gone to bed. Assistance was soon obtained, and information was sent to the Warrington Fire Brigade, but in the meantime Mr. James Hampton arrived with the Thelwall Parish Council fire hose, and poured a steady stream of water on to the flames. Other willing workers appeared; and to their services May be attributed.the fact that the, fire did not spread to the whole of the barns, and to the outbuildings, in addition to the house itself. They were particularly useful in rescuing the cattle and horses from danger. It may be added that the Warrington brigade, in charge of Deputy-Superintendent Cook, rendered very useful service.

div.head: PRIVATE S. BRAZENDALE.
div.p: PRIVATE S. BRAZENDALE.
Village Patriot Has Military Funeral

div.head: At Parish Church.
div.p: At Parish Church.
"I HAVE DONE MY DUTY."

Amidst manifestations of sorrow,' one of I.ymm's patriotic sons, Private Stanley Brazen dale, was laid to rest in the Parish Churchyard' on Wednesday afternoon: As a. tribute to "his memory practically the whole of: the -Villagers were to be seen at the: graveside, '.and most: of, the shops and .works in the vicinity ivere closedi for the occasiOn. ' The circumstances of Private Brazendale's death have created a painful impression, his parents having no idea that he was so seriously ill; in fact a letter was received from him by his sister on the day of his death (last Friday), and written the day previoply. Private Stanley Brazendale, • twenty-three years of age, was exceedingly well liked through-

div.head: LATE PRIVATE BRAZENDALh.
div.p: THE LATE PRIVATE BRAZENDALh.

out the village for his genial disposition and endearing good nature. A member of as fine a patriotic family we have as yet recorded, it was no surprise to his parents and associates that he should enlist in the sth . Cheshires at the outbreak of war, especially as he was member of the local "Terriers." . After the necessary training in several parts of the country he was drafted to the Front fouiteen months ago, and witnessed many stirring engagements. He has never had a furlough ° since he went out to France. A week or so ago his parents received the news that he had landed in England, hav- ing been sent home through a serious illness. " Keep On Smiling."

As already stated, the last letter received was written' the day prior to his -death, and the following are extracts :7-" I am pleased to receive your letter of the 9th' lust., and 'to know that you are quite well.and„happy. About my- self, I am not 'feeling very well just now, but it is no use being. downhearted. I dare .say you have been 'wondering what has been the matter with me. Unfortunately I have to be operated upon. I have to have a small bone taken from the back- of my head. They will not let me go abroad again, so 'dear, at least I have done my duty. I shall not be called a coward like some of the slackers in England who won't Come up and show themselves. I shall be pleased to see you again, but am afraid it won't be for twO or three months yet. I wish I were a little nearer home so that you might come and see me, but never mind, keep on smiling." The first intimation of his death was con- veyed to his parents by Private Kirk, attached to the same regiment, this being quickly fol- lowed by a telegram from .the Nottingham General Hospital, where Private Brazendale was lying. In civilian life he was employed as a teams- man under Mr:.:VV. Shakeshaft, of Higher-lane, Lymm, and was a faithful worshipper at the Lymm . Parish Church. / He was greatly esteemed by the-schoolboys in the district, for

in his spare moments he taught many of them the advantages of Swedish drill. His remains were carried by a detachment of the local Home Defence Corps, fully 20 members taking part in the procession. The bearers were :—Captain G. R. Williamson, Sergeant S. D. Moston, Sergeant G. L. Farrar, Privates G. Parker, J. Burn, F. Morris, T. Jones 'Parry, J. G. Cooke, F. W. Druce, E. N. Owen, W. H. Rose and T. Jeeves. •• . Part of the National Reserve from Winwick were in attendance, and fired volleys over their dead comrade's grave. • A Soldier Family. •

The late Private Brazendale's parents reside at Tower. Cottages, Lymm, his mother having been married twice, and from this good lady the information was gleaned that her son was only one of a joint family of seven who have past and present fought for England and home. Her late husband, Private William Brazendale, was for a great number of years with the 14th Lions, a regiment which we believe is . now e:- tinct. He saw, no foreign service et delighted .to speak a the ,good old 'days when England 'Was at peace. Her son, Private'Ernest Brazen- dale,' who is at present training in England with the sth Cheshires, was in' the clean and tidy home when our representative called. Asked if he bad any idea of when he would be sent to the Front, he just replied f` I do not know, but I am ready whenever it may be." Another lady of the household is Mrs. , James Buchanan, a sister of the deceased, whose husband is .at pre- sent serving with Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. Nearly eight months ago he thought it was, his duty to assist the Motherland, and was eventually sent to England, his wife and one child travelling with him. He was drafted to the Front three months ago. Mrs. Harrison has also a stepson, Private William Harrison, facing the foe. Journeying to the Front in the early part of September, he has been through may severe engagements with the R.F.A. Letters received from him are all of the cheery type, and have in more ways than one helped to ease the present burden of his sorrowing parents. Two cousins of the deceased, Privates Joseph and George Brazendale, are serving in France, and went out with Stanley at the same time. Just now this patriotic family are passing through a time of adversity, and especially Mrs. Harrison, for .added to her present sorrow is ,the fact that her brother-in-' law, Private Alfred Goodwin, attached. to a Manchester regiment, is reported missing. No news has been forthcoming of his whereabouts for the last five 'months.

div.head: NATION'S DEPENDENTS.
div.p: THE NATION'S DEPENDENTS.
How Lymm Has Attended To Their Wants.

/ Fifteen months of highly useful work in con- nection with the Soldiers' and Sailors' Families' Association in Lymm and district is reviewed by the Rev. 'G. R. Thurston, chairman and hon. treasurer of the branch, in a report which has just .been issued. He states that the .branch was opened soon after the outbreak of war, and the following were appointed to administer relief: Rev. G. B. Thurston (chairman and hon. treasurer; Mr. F. E. Evans (hon. secretary),, Dr. H. *A. Bur- rowes, Mr. J. G. Lister Farrar, Rev. E. E. Lovell, Eymm; Mr. W. G. Lumb, Oughtrington; and Rev. G. Egerton Warburton,- Warburton.

The attendan-de of the committee has been ex- cellent, all the members evincing not merely keen interest, but a thorough grasp of the work- ing ,of the association. The assistance rendered by the association in Lymm and, district has been of a two-fold character, namely, financial. and, what has proved to be even more valuable. the giving of advice in many circumstances where a sound and well-informed friend was needed. Most of this latter work has fallen to the lot of the hon. secretary, Who has dealt with over two hundred cases,- filling up necessary forms and dispatching to the proper quarters, getting claims adjusted, tracing missing and wounded soldiers; looking after- the 'effects of those who have fallen in battle, paying out weekly grants, and generally supervising in a most efficient manner the work of the associa- tion.

Twenty-two wives, forty-nine children, and nineteen dependents have received financial, aid. In most cases separation allowance has not come to hand till some time has elapsed after the departure of husband or son; here, the association has rendered valuable aid in advanc- ing the prospective weekly allowance, and a considerable.amount has been refunded by those assisted. Arrangements have also been made for six Prisoners of war of the Cheshire Regi- ment to receive parcels -Of food and clothing each fortnight. In a statement of accounts it. is mentioned that £93 19s. 7d. was spent in the assisting of cases, along with £2. 18s. 10d. for special grants.

Only Two Lamps Left.

At the meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee on Tuesday evening, the Acting Clerk (Mr. W. E. Hough) read a letter. which he had received from Mr.. W. S. had- dock, general manager of the Warrington Cor- poration Gas Department, who stated that he had estimated the cost of lighting 27 to 39 lamps at Stockton Heath with controllers and No. 3 Kern burners. If the lamps were lighted from half an hour after sunset, and extinguished at eleven o'clock, the price would be 40s. per lamp per annum. If the lamps were lighted at 5,30 in the morning from the Ist November to the 28th February, and extinguished half an hour before sunrise the charge would be 2s. per lamp extra. The estimate was based on the present price of gas, but, owing to abnormal conditions, he might hare to increase the price or reduce it. Every penny difference in the price of gas would increase or decrease the cost per lamp 64. per annum. The calculations had been based on the actual times of sunrise and sunset in War- rington, which was not the same as at Green- wich. Mr. Hough added that the police super- intendent had called. his. attention to the light- ing of Stockton Heath, and had expressed the opinion that there were too many lights in the parish at present. div.head: TRENCHES.
div.p: TRENCHES.
"OH, THE LANGUAGE!"
Dug-Out Banquet Which Turned Out
To Be Biscuits And Water.

Bombardier Entwistle, who relinquished his post on the teaching staff at St. Barnabas' School to join the R.F.A., states in an enter- taining. letter to a friend : " Instead of using London omnibuses this time, we came up the line on the gee-gees. On the way we lost our mascot. We had adopted a puppy, a little wee terrier which one of the chaps had -fished out of the Somme. It took distemper and died .at my feet as I was on picket two nights ago. . • "We have a nice little dug-out. It goes about 14ft. under ground, so that even in the clay time we have a light. One can just stand up- right. and it is, about sft. wide. It iS- our hotel, where we shall live for several weeks. Our horses we shall not see. They are away behind us. We have another room to our sulk, but, as it is scarcely habitable, we only use it as a cookhouse. Thereby hangs a tale of woe. "To-night we are waiting for the cart to bring' our rations. It can only come In the dark, and we are just promising ourselves a feast—hot tea, real bread, and, perhaps, butter and jam, and, maybe, toasted cheese. We have scouted for some wood, dried it, chopped it, .and made a fire, which we had to relight several times. It is getting on towards eight o'clock now, but, never mind, we shall have such a tea. The -cart has come and we have, lugged the goods off. Now the water -cart has- come along. and filled our barrel, up. The bung has got lost; so we have had to carry /the barrel back instead of rolling it. It has, fallen into the mud' a few times.

div.head: Banquet Which Was Not.
div.p: The Banquet Which Was Not.

"Over, the fire .we have fried some bacon and. Init à diiie a water' on. to bdil. It has taken a long time. We have. fanned that blaze until. we are like chimney sweeps • "-It is now nearly 10: o'clock. We have. cooked the bacon in a dixie lid, and have put. over the water to keep warm. "But I would butt in and take the water off the fire, only to see the tea upset, and the bacon, go in the water, and, of course, queer the pitch!. Visions of a banquet dispelled! There is none! But oh, the language! Sure the Germans heard it. Then we stood up and laughed like a pack of hyenas. We filed back like mourners, and' fared sumptuously on biscuits, jam and water:. •We are looking forward to breakfast I can tell 3riven."

div.head: PRIVATE B. OLDROYD
div.p: PRIVATE B. OLDROYD
Tells How He Sniped An bidusizious
German.

Private B. Oldroyd, of the Argyle and Suther- land Highlanders, in a letter to his wife, re- siding at 86, Wellington-street, says:—" We have had a terrible time these last 12 days in the trenches. The Germans bombarded, us un- mercifully night .and day, and also blew up a mine just on our left. I had another very narrow escape on Sunday night. I was on sentry duty on the firestep, when a rifle grenade dropped right in front of me, just about a foot away, and, would you believe it, it never ex- ploded. When I got my breath back, I put my hand out to get the grenade, and a sniper's bul- let went past my `napper' into a sandbag: He must have been very smart. The next morning I was at the sniper's .plate when I saw •a big German knocking a post down with a mallet, so. I put My rifle through the hole in the plate and. let him have 'One.' I was ready to fire again, but the first one did him, for he was either wounded or killed outright: and I saw the Mallet fall from his hand. . . . We are having it very cold here, there being a thick frost every morn- ing. You can send' The Examiner' if you like. I like reading it, for it makes one feel at home."

div.p: IS HE A GERMAN?
Suspect Arrested hi Refresh-

SAID HE WAS AN AMERICAN.

In applying for an adjournment of a case in connectioa with an offence under the Aliens' Registration Act, at the Borough Court on Wed- nesday, the Chief Constable pointed out that the police had very strong reasons to believe that the accused was a German and was not registered. _ _

The accused gave his name as John Henry Steeler, and as he was only arrested on Tuesday night, the police were desirous of instituting inquiries. A remand of eight days was granted by the magistrates. The Chief Constable said that prisoner had been employed at a local works and had lodged at the Working Men's Refreshment Rooms in llorsemarket-street, where he was arrested by Detectivo-Sergeant Reddington. The police were of the opinion that prisoner was of German Parents, and it was his duty, on coming into the town from Manchester on Monday to comply wit'h the registration order. When arrested by Sergeant Reddington he claimed that he was an American. Prisoner said he did not know until the detective officer questioned him that he ought to have registered. The Chief Constable: It is useless to make that excuse. He knew perfectly well all about it. . Detective-Sergeant Reddington, who proved the arrest, said that at the Police Station pris- (Hier said he knew he ought to have registered.

div.head: "MODERN PAINTERS."
div.p: "MODERN PAINTERS."

"When the prisoner and her husband come into the town they paint it red," remarked the 'Chief Constable (Mr. Martin Nicholls) at the Borough Police Court on Monday, when an elderly and unkempt woman named Elizabeth Longshaw, of no settled abode, pleaded guilty •to stealing 4-Ib. of ham from Mrs. McCabe's shop at 1, St. Austin's-lane.

The daughter of the prosecutor saw the prisoner walking out of the shop 'with the ham in her hand, amil pushed her back again until her mother arrived. Later the police appeared. 'The Chief Constable' said that since 1890 the prisoner, had been convicted sixteen times at Warrington, and had servtql several sentences for stealing. Sentence: Three months' imprisonment.

div.head: CORNER IN PORK.
div.p: CORNER IN PORK.
nig Theft From Slaughter-house Late At Night.

Charles Lamb's successor as a passionate lover of roast pig has been discovered in War- rington. He is Frederick William Price, of 39, Clegg-street. This fact was revealed at the Borough Court on Monday, when Price confessed to ,stealing 701 b. of pork, value VA, the property of Richard C. Shaw, butcher, of 104, Orford-lane. It was explained by the Chief Constable that the pork—three legs of a pig—was stolen from the slaughter-house in Clegg-street by the Prisoner late on Saturday night. Inspector Stuart made inquiries and, when standing out- side of the prisoner's house, heard him say to his wife, "Put plenty of salt on them and rub it in. They will keep." The Inspector found two of the legs on the kitchen table and the other in a bedroom. The Prisoner: I was out of work, had had a drop of beer, and was a bit desperate. The Chief Constable: He took such a lot that he must have expected to be out of work a long while. The reason he did not take more was probably because he could not carry it.
Fine: 405., or, in default, a month's imprison- ment.

AND BIRCH-ROD.
Boys Get Different Punishment For
Theft.

Another batch of juvenile offenders made their appearance at the Police Court on Wed- nesday. Three boys, whose ages were between eleven and twelve years, were summoned for stealing various small articles from Messrs. Woolworth's, Sankey-street, and from stalls in the market. The booty included scissors, safety razors,

div.head: Lack of Control.
div.p: Lack of Control.

Mr. Moore Murray (Director of _Education) said he felt that control at borne was lacking, with the boys. •Last year one of them was marked down in the school register as not being trustworthy. At that time the boy's step- mother expressed the wish to the headmaster that she would be glad if the boy were sent away. In his opinion it was this boy who had led the other two into trouble. The step-mother of the boy stated that she had been given to understand that he had obtained money for running errands, and had bought the toys in that way The boy particularly referred to was sent to a reformatory until he is 16 years of age, and the other two boys were ordered to receive six strokes with the birch-rod. div.head: BEYOND CONTROL.
div.p: BEYOND CONTROL.
Domestic Sent To Gaol For Three Months.

"Prison is the only place to bring her to her -Senses," was the remark of the Chief Constable addressed about a young woman .named Teresa Goddard, who was charged at the Police Court on Wednesday with stealing a blanket and other articles, value 2.3, the property of Thos. Read, 74, -New-road. , It was stated that the prosecutor, out of sym- pathy for the girl, engaged her as a domestic until such time as she was able to secure another appointment. Recently he had occasion to visit the Infirmary ,'and left the house in the afternoon; the key of the house being given int ) the charge of a neighbour. During his absence the girl obtained the key, entered the house, and stole the property, which was afterwards disposed of in the nature of gifts, whilst some found its way to the pawnshop. The police had been successful in recovering the whole of the property. The Chief Constable said the girl appeared to be absolutely beyond control. Everything pos- sible .had been done to induce her to reform. In November, 1914, she was before the Court, charged with stealing a lady's gold ring, and the magistrates let her off. Last December she was again before the Court on a charge of steal- ing lady's clothing, and she was again leniently dealt with. Since the adjournment, efforts had been made to get her to go into a home, but she preferred to go to prison. The magistrates sent her to gaol for three months.

div.head: BY-TURN PUDDLER.
div.p: BY-TURN PUDDLER.
Man's Plea For Neglect Of Work Rejected.

"I am a by-turn puddler and no manager or firm has any claim on me," declared Samuel Lamb, of 21, Plumpton-street, at the Munitions Tribunal on• Monday, when he was charged with absenting himself without leave on the 31st ult. The manager said that Lamb had been re- peitedly warned about not fulfilling his duties. He was earning 10s. 6d. or lls, a turn. He entirely ignored the regulations issued by the Government and, by his neglect, had caused the firm and the men employed with him to lose a lot of money. Lamb asserted that as he was a by-turn man a case could not be made out against him. Another man looked after the furnace. The manager replied that Lamb had not been a by-turn puddler for 21 years.
When tlie Court fined Lamb £l, he retorted that he would not pay so much, but "would stand 10s."
"The money will be deducted from your wages in instalments of ss. per week," re- marked Mr. T. J. Ridgway, who presided.

Business Gentleman's Narrow

div.head: CONSIDERABLE DAMAGE.
div.p: CONSIDERABLE DAMAGE.
Warrington was shaken by wind, rain and thunder on Wednesday.
_ . Most property proved stable, but, of course, there was the usual profuse alienating of slates from roofs.

In one quarter, however, serious damage was done, a chimney-stack, 70 feet high, standing on the premises of Messrs. T. and H. Beddard, firewood manufacturers, of John-street, War- rington, collapsing suddenly. Thirty or forty tons of bricks were scattered fiercely at the adjoining houses and into vari- ous parts of the works. A considerable quan- tity dropped on to the engine house, destroying the roof in a twinkling and burying Mr. Thos. Beddard in the debris. Naturally, as soon as the. chimney began to fall, the workmen rushed away, but on ' hearing cries for help by Mr. Beddard, a party returned, and dug. him out at great peril to themselves. Mr. Beddard re- ceived attention and,.was then taken: home in a eab. A .shoulder blade, was .discovered to have been broken and he was bruised all 'over,' but we are pleased to say he is progressing well. As the chimney toppled over hundreds of bricks were flung against the houses within range. The outhouses at Gartland's and Thorley', in John-street, were completely de- molished, and several windows in the houses were broken. Two houses, occupied by Mr. Lee and Mr. Crozier, also suffered, the windows in the back kitchens being penetrated. Mrs. Gartland happened to be in the yard at the time, and, on seeing the chimney falling, raised her hands to protect her head. In doing so her hands were badly cut. It may be added that the chimney had. not been used for some time. The damage done to the machinery and various other parts of the works is eonSiclerable.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.
THE TOWN'S AMBMON.
Captain Says They Will Make It A Leading Club.
MAY BECOME LIMITED LIABILITY
COMPANY.

Gratified and fortified by the extensive sup- port the new Warrington Town Club has re- ceived, George Whitfield, the captain, told an "Examiner" representative the other night that the committee and players are determined to place the club in the front rank of Associa- tion teams, and so make the town an important Association centre. _ _

Before the year is out," he added, "i think we shall make the club a limited liability company, the same as most of those of the better class. The funds are beginning to go up now, and we are past the time when we only just paid our way. We are very pleased With the support given. "We are willing to take a field for a lease of a number of years. This we shall enclose and erect stands, &c., as opportunity occasions —perhaps at the beginning of next season— though, of course, the war may alter Our plans. One never knows, but one is hopeful.

div.head: Keen Lot.
div.p: A Keen Lot.
"All the committee and players are ken and there is not one who would not give forth his best in the interests, of the club.

"You might note the fact that we have decided to don green and scarlet jerseys, dis- carding completely the blue and white, which, until Saturday, Warringtonians have only seen us in since we have been in the Combination. Before we became affiliated With the Combina- tion we used to wear the green and scarlet frequently. We consider them our lucky colours, for we have certainly done well when wearing them. • To Strengthen the Front. Line.

"I have great faith in the team. Generally, it is strong, but there is weakness in the for- ward line. However, as soon as we are able to re-arrange that we shall be ready for any club in the Combination. In my opinion the other lines are all . right and do not require disturbing. I have several good players in my eye 'for the front line, but do not expect we shall get them until next season. They live out of town, and, when a club is just beginning to feel its feet,. we .have, to consider expenses very carefully... But we shall certainly have a stronger line next season.;"

"Who, in your opinion, are the best players, besides yourself?" ,asked our representative. "Kite is as good a goalkeeper as we could possibly have as a 'local.' Although only 20 years old, Millward is shaping very promis- ingly at left-back, and, if he has luck, I think he will do well in the football world. He is a hard worker, full of courage and versatile in his methods. Forwards have to be particularly smart to get past him. They cannot anticipate his tactics."
The Captain's Fine Record.

Then, of course, there is the captain himself. Of him let us speak ourselves. Whitfield has been in good class football since he was 20 years of age (he is now 30 and his men look upon him with the respect his skill and experi- ence should engender. Whitfield has a nice

div.head: NORTHERN UNION'S PROTEST ABOUT DAINTITH.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION'S PROTEST ABOUT DAINTITH.

Walkden Again Beaten. Mr. Peter Peacock, jun., the chairman of War- rington. Town, informs me that there is some trouble between themselves and the Northern Union Club re " Shint "! Daintith playing for the Town without permission, and, therefore, he will not .figure in to-day's match.

The men to be selected- from to meet Eccles Borough at Hood-lane are: Berry (Everton), Leah, Cookson, G. Whitfield, Ditchfield, Os- borne, Aspinall, T. Whitfield, Foster, Shake- shaft, Millward, Banner, Illidge, and Sack Broster.

The last-named is starting with a good repu- tation to his credit, having played for Queen's Park Rangers. He will figure, in the .half-back line. I may add that there are prospects that Gee, of Oldham, will be coming to us soon. Berry is taking Percy Kite's place in goal owing to the latter's marrin;.;(• to Miss Ada Brereton at Stockton Heath to-day. In the Eccles team will appear W. Siddall, who assisted the Town at the commencement of the season. He will require watching.

Last Saturday we recorded our first home victory. It was not obtained without a strenu- ous effort. A drawn game seemed certain until a few minutes from time, when Aspinall notched the winning goal. The home players have only themselves to blame for not achiev- ing a more substantial victory. When they had established a clear lead of two goals and had taken the measure of their opponents they began to relax their efforts. This almost proved their downfall, for Walkden, taking advantage of their laxity, put on a couple of _goals in as many minutes.

The sudden change in their foxtune drove Warrington to desperation and there was more vigour than science displayed in the closing stages, but the winning goal in the last, few seconds restored their exuberant spirits. It is to be hoped the lesson will not be forgotten by the Warrington players on future occasions.

Considering the many opportunities which came the way of the home players the score does not reflect great credit on their marksmaft. ship in front of goal. Before the interval they ought to have been three goals up at least. The spectators were beginning to despair whether there was a player who could hit the target, so many chances were allowed to go -a -begging. It was only on rare'occasions that the Warring- ton defence was seriously troubled, for the half- backs and full-backs did .not allow, the visiting forwards to develop a sustained attack.

The introduction of Osborne at full-back, who formerly assisted the old Warrington Albion Club, has strengthened the defence. Under pressure he was very cool, and, with Millward playing so consistently, the club are well served in that department. The first goal was a really class shot, for Ditchfield, obtaining possession fully twenty yards from the goal- line, took deliberate aim. and piloted the ball in the top corner of the net After so many f:, ilures the goal came as a welcome tonic to the spec- tators, and they clamoured for more, but the Walkden custodian proved his worth by cleverly saving shots from Poster and Aspinall.

If the first half lacked excitement there was enough to satisfy the spectators in the second. Warrington soon asserted their superiority, and after prolonged pressure Aspinall added a second goal. There were repeated failures on the part of the home forwards, and one won- dered whether the unevenness of thi, turf was responsible for the futile efforts to find the net. At this stage Warrington allowed matters to drift and they seemed perfectly satisfied with their lead until a mistake by the home backs let in Lord, who beat Kite with a splendid drive. Warrington had hardly recovered when a penalty for "hands" gave Walkden a second goal., Kite saved the shot, but lost possession, and, the penalty-taker regaining the ball, made no mistake with the secOnd attempt. With the scores equal Warrington made 'determined efforts to regain the lead, Aspinall eventually scoring amidst great excitement

The appearance of "Shint" Daintith, the Rugger half-back, in the Town team caused much speculation. Ile was quite at home in the middle line and adapted himself to his new surroundings. He gave a very sound dis- play. Before he was attracted to the, handling code Daintith learned his football with an Association team. George Whitfield is now getting into his stride and there was a vast improvement in his play. His judgment in placing the ball to the forwards was a marked feature. He was ably supported by the diminutive Ditchfield, whose tireless', energy, both in atthck and defence, was very notice- able.

Of the forwards, Midge was entirely off his game and Banner suffered in consequence. The best wing was Foster and Aspinall. The latter is a rare worker and he gave the visitors' defence a warm time. T. Whitfield at centre spoiled his best work by his poor shooting.
In goal Kite was not over-worked, but was always ready when called upon. A particu- larly clever clearance was in the first half, when he dealt with a high shot in masterly style.

div.head: GAME DESCRIBED.
div.p: THE GAME DESCRIBED.

It will be remembered that it was against the Walkden Central the previous week that the Town team obtained their initial victory in the competition, and after gaining both points on foren soil, by the score Of five goals against two, the home supporters were very confident that we should secure another couple of points in comfortable fashion. Unfortunately, the Town Club were not able to call upon the same players owing to accidents .and other causes. Leah and Cookson- were. unable to .turn out, and this caused a re-arrangement- of the team, Millward again appearing at full-back" and being partnered by Osborne.. The latter. a, Warrington player, formerly assisted the War- grington Albion 'and the Everton Reserve team. Foster wa4 brought in at the centre-forward ,position. Owing to, the late arrival of the visitors a start was not made until forty-five minutes behind the official time, when the fol- lowing players lined out, under the control of Mr. Bragg, Manchester Warrington Town: Kite; Osborne and Mill- ward; Daintith, G. Whitfield and Ditchfield; Aspinall, T. Whitfield, Foster, Illidge and Banner.
Walkden Central: Harding; Marsden and Berry; Meehan, Mather and Cookson; Hodg- kinson, Short, Lord, Brooks and Hayes.
There were 2,000 spectators.

_ Foster set the ball rolling, ,and after easy exchanges by the defenders -Ditchfield, by a well-judged pass, enabled the home forwards to make the first Atack. ,Illidge and Banner, showing goal understanding,' the ball was dropped into the centre, where T. Whitfield was only inches on the wrong side of the post with a fast drive. The visitors responded to this in spirited style, Hayes leading the way,
but when within shouting distance Brooks failed to make the best of his chances and shot wide. -

Froth the goal-kick the home forwards paid a brief visit to the visitors' end, where Marsden very smartly robbed T. Whitfield, when the latter was in the act of shooting. A corner to the 'visitors was cleared by Whitfield, and Foster eluded the attentions of Mather, but his final effort went to the wrong side of the upright, and a little • later a good attempt by Daintith was only inches wide.

div.p: THE FOOTBALL FIEL‘,.
AND COMMENTS _AMONG THE LOCALS.

Che- shire Senior Cup medal, two Cheshire Senior runners-up medals, Manchester Junior Cup medal, and five Altrincham Cup medals. The medals obtained in Altrincham indicate his connection with that town. lie played for Altrincham for several years and had the honour of being captain of the club five times. Before going to Altrincham he figured pro- minently with Denton. Whilst with Altrinc- ham he played in two Cheshire v. Whitfield has conducted .himself well in all positions on the field—excluding goal—but his favourite place is that of centre-half. There he will continue playing for the Town; and may good luck attend both him and his company!

div.head: In the Homo Half.
div.p: In the Homo Half.

A visit to the home half was quickly repulsed by Millward. and, directly afterwards, offside against Aspinall gave relief to the visitors' defence. The visiting forwards now took play to the borne end, where offside against Short caused them to be sent back, and later the same player missed a very easy chance of scor- ing by hesitating, and allowed Millward to clear well with a big kick, this being followed by a strong attack on the Walkden goal, which resulted in Ditchfield scoring a splendid goal from twenty-five yards' range. Had it not been for the good play by 'Hard- ing, Marsden and Berry, other goals would have followed very soon. The home forwards, at this juncture, were well supported by their half-backs. Eventually Marsden raised the siege with a big clearance, and a long shot by Cookson which appeared to be going wide was curled in by the wind and Kite just tipped the ball over the bar. The corner-kick was easily cleared and Foster tested Harding with a low shot, which was successfully dealt with. Hayes transferred play and .caused, trouble to Kite to save his charge. Half-time:— Warrington Town, I goal.

Walkden Central, 0. On resuming, the visitors rearranged their team, the outside wing players exchanging positions and Mather and Lord' following suit, while Illidge went inside-right for the home team. The changes proved to be well made, for the visitors were quickly on the aggressive, and Mather was near the mark with _a good shot The visitors were having the best of the ex- changes, and. Millward and Osborne were dis- playing good form in defence. ' Another attack by the -home forwards, saw Aspinalr skim the bar with a great shot Mid- field play was the erder for few minutes, and then Aspinall again, led an attack on the visi- tors' goal, where Harding saved from a crowd of players. Good combination, in midfield by the visitors resulted in Kite saving easily and trans- ferring the leather to his own forwards. Foster gave Harding- a warm 'shot to deal with. The attack was continued, and Aspinall gained the second goal for the home team. From the centre-kick the visitors' retaliated very strongly, and good play-by Hodgkinscrn resulted in Hayes scoring the first point for the visitors. Encour- aged by this success, the visitors made strong efforts to get on equal terms, and, from another centre by Hodgkinson, Osborne was ,penalised for bands. • Short was entrusted -with the kick, and Kite was not able to effect a proper clear- ance.' The first named. followed up and' netted the ball and made the scores equal. Changes and Exchanges.

Aspinall now changed to the inside position, and following some keen excimnges, he succeeded in beating Harding With a low drive, and thus gained the lead for the home team. The above teams met last week on the Arpley ground: The Mersey captain won.the toss, but it was not Of 'much benefit- owing to a.strong cross wind. div.head: Effect Of The New Regulations On Licensees And Others.
div.p: Effect Of The New Regulations On Licensees And Others.
LITTLE DEMAND FOR NON- INTOXICANTS.

The first day of the new drinking Order was wet, cold and miserable, and those inclined for " a wee doch and doris " in one of the licensed houses were denied the privilege, at least before the hour of -twelve. Paying a visit to those hostels which had opened for the sale of non- intoxicants, one found only a few straggling habitues of the tavern imbibing hot drinks, such as Bovril, coffee and tea, which, as one licensee 'remarked," izlid not pay to keep the water hot." Only a few coppers were taken at one house be- fore 12 noon on Monday, ivhilst at another the total takings were is. 4T-Is. for billiards and 4d. for non-intoxicants.

Some workmen who were, previous to the Act, accustomed to their morning refresher, as they termed it, were loud and indignant in their protest against the new regulations, whilst many others openly remarked that they meant to make up for it during the dinner hour. Asking of a " commercial " from Liverpool what he thought of the new Act, one was vouch- safed the reply that what was good for Liver- pool was equally good for Warrington, and that he (the speaker) did not think any difficulty would arise over the rather stringent new law. According to what •he had heard from pro- prietors of licensed houses in those areas affected, the landlords had had no really serious complaints or disturbances. Workmen had adapted themselves to the new law with praiseworthy distinction, and the same would, he felt sure, equally apply to those districts lately scheduled. No Treating and No Slate.

Curiously enough the majority of grumbles heard were not so much against the late open- ing of houses as against that clause dealing with the no-treating question. • The. typical British workman is usually generous to a fault, Much the same as his con- frere in- Russia and the very fact of his not being able to "stand a drink" to his fellow comrades seems to him unfair and a trespass on his liberties.

Yet it is this "standing treat" which has in the past accounted for much of the excess of drinking. Certain it is that the new rule will do away with the system of booking on the " slate " until the week-end, which system in the past has been both obnoxious to the licensee. in,the homes. and to the man himself. PronrietArs of hostelries are, just now yulhng wry faces. They complain that the new regulations are much too drastic, yet with philosophy are carrying the extra burdens brought about by the war with calmness and resolve. Better Time.

Inquiries of fieveral works 'managers elicit the fact that already the percentage of work- men not turning in to work has diminished con- siderable, which can, they state, be attributed to the new Order.

div.head: NOT SATISFIED.

Chief Constable Says Lights Must Be Lower.
OTHERWISE, PROSECUTION

Although generally the lighting Order has been obeyed, some shopkeepers and many householders have dissatisfied the Chief Con- stable (Mr. Martin Nicholls) to such an extent that he has asked "The Examiner" again to warn delinquents that units& their lights be subdued prosecutions will follow. Under the Defence of the Realm Act magistrates have power to inflict severe penalties. The warning should be immediately heeded. The Order, even so far as it has yet been observed, has had a remarkable eoect upon the appearance of the borough. Drapers have been bombarded with customers, and every building should soon be a "House of the green blinds." Thursday night's glimmer in the town was what is really desired. All the shopkeepers wery taking their half-holiday. Not a flare of light was to be seen through any window, excepting the flicker which helps a policeman to discover burglars when on his midnight rounds. The moon was obscured by thick clods, and rain fell fiercely upon wayfarers. The electric and gas lamps were mere landmarks instead of lighters of. the way, and pedestrians collided with each other with pardonable frequency. Everywhere was dismal, murky, and mournful. Visibly, -from aloft, Warrington was off the map. It was an ideal example of what we should always be under the lighting Order. What householders should bear in mind is that bright light at the rear of their premises is as fatal as at the front. This fact seems to have been overlooked in many quarters. Every one must obey the Order. Failure on the part of a few may be fatal to the welfare of the town. It is the leaks in the ship which cause it to sink. It will be the streaks of light which 'will enable us to be detected. .

div.p: CHURCH SERVICES.
The Clergy Discuss Advisability Of Early Evensong.'

- A representative gathering of local clergymen, at the Rectory on Tuesday evening, discussed, under the presidency of the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), who, had called the meeting, the inethoda.to be adopted by churches to comply with the new Lighting Order. There. Were several distinct lines of thought. Some were in favour of darkening windows and proceeding with the services as usual; some of holding an evening service of curtailed length; and some of holding afternoon services and dis- pensing with the expense of lighting up and the danger of assembling in large bodies in the even- ing. . • _. .

div.head: The. Bishop's Advice..
div.p: The. Bishop's Advice..

..The Rotor read the letter which the Bishop of Liverpool has sent to the clergy of the diocese, pointing • out that compliance with the new regulations is compulsory. It was not ". may," but a must." In some churches it might be ,pos- sible to carry out the Order by the use of cur- tains and dark blinds. Where it was not, it would be necessary for the evening service to close .not later than p. 30 from the present date until the middle of March, and not later than 710 during the succeeding month. Afternoon v. Evening Services.

The Rector said the clergy and wardens of the Parish' Church had come to the unanimous conclusion last week that the best course was to hold the Sunday evening service at 6.30, the same time as before, and to darken the windows —as they could do without any difficulty—by closing the galleries and introducing blinds for the lower windows. It had since been repre- sented to him that at churches where it was not easy to darken the windows, the holding of the services at an earlier hour might lead to al falling off in the congregation, unless there wasl a uniform time for the whole town. He had, therefore, convened that meeting, and if a unanimous conclusion were . arrived at, the Roman Cath9lic clergy and Nonconformist ministers could, if they thought well, take similar action. The wardens of the Parish Church had reconsidered the matter, and if that meeting came to a unanimous decision, they would be willing for the next month to hold the ISunday evening service at 5.30 instead of at 6.30. He received a letter from the Rev. .11. B. Firth, stating that it, had been decided to hold the ser- vice at St. James' Church, Latchford, at 6 o'clock for the next few weeks. It was expected that by having curtailed evensong and a short sermon, the congregation would be out of church by 6.50. He had had other expressions of opinion, and he again called his wardens to- gether. It was then decided that should that meeting come to a unanimous resolve they would be willing to have service at the Parish Church at 5.30 instead of 6.30. Afternoon Arrangements.

The Rev. James Davies said that on the re- ceipt of the Bishop's letter his church council and Sunday school teachers decided that five o'clock, being tea-time, would he very incon- venient, And that ,3.30 would be the most suit- able. They tried it last Sunday, and found it convenient.. If they could not diminish their light by darkening the very large window's at St. Ann's they thought it advisable to get to work at once, as the Germans would not recog- nise February 16th as the date for their next visit to this country. (Laughter.) In April they could return to the usual hours. The Rev. E. Downham said it was impossible to shade the windows of St. Paul's Church, which stood in a prominent position. At first they considered the advisability of having a service from 5.30 to 6.30, with only one psalm, lesson and canticle, but that was tea-time, and they concluded to have service from 3.30 to 4.30. The Young Men's Bible Class agreed that it was a splendid idea, for they would be able to come straight from the class to the church. He did not think it was a. question of shading the windows only. The spirit of the Order was the desire to prevent people from gathering in numbers, and if anything happened at one of the churches through going against that spirit, they would never forgive themselves, when at a little sacrifice they could have prevented it ' by holding the services, as our fathers did, at an earlier hour. The Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth said that at St. Barnabas' Church he and the wardens had already discussed this matter and had decided that it was possible to shade the windows, and to hold the evening service on Sunday at the usual hour. The order had been given, and he', could not now countermand it. If evensong ' were 'held in the afternoon on Sunday, to be logical the weeknight Lenten services would have to be stopped, too. He did not think the present was the time for taking away what might be helpful to the demotion of some—per- hoes only a few. He considered it would be safe to hold evening service, as timely warning of Zeppelins being in our neighbourhood would be given. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton was of the opihion that as the circumstances differed in the various parishes, a great deal would have to be left to the discretion of the clergy and warekens. They had not decided upon any change at Holy Trinity Church. but if uniform action were con- sidered desirable they would try to fall in with it. He thought, however, they would be able effectively to shade their windowtf, which were,

hawever.- most thick and onanue. Mr. Reddish ,stated that the globes in St. Peter's Church had been shaded, and the clergy and wardens favoured the idea of continuing the service at the same hour as before. If, however, there was to be a uniforT change,
three o'clock would be preferable to 5.30.
Picture Palaces and Theatres.

The Rev. T. Vickers said the incumbent and wardens of each parish knew their particular circumstances, and would be in a poeition to make their own arrangements. At St. Clement's Mission they had decided to hold shortened evensong at six o'clock, and he was afraid it could not be altered now. The Rev. J. M. Buckmaster said, with regard to the question of safety, when the police found it necessary to insist upon an early closing of picture palaces and theatres, which on six days of the week were allowed to be open until ten o'clock at night, it would be time enough to consider whether the churches were in any danger in keeping people together on one day of the week until 7.30. for it. -The.Rev. S. G. Stanton did not think there would be any material gain from uniformity in the matter. On the occasion of the recent air raid the transmission of official telephone messages of urgent importance was seriously interfered with at several places by the inconsiderate and un- necessary use of the telephone by private sub- scribers to call up the police and other. public officials. The Postmaster-General earnestly appeals to the public to use the telephone as little as pos- sible on such occasions, and on no account to call up the police or other public officials on unimportant or merely, personal matters. If this warning is not regarded it may become necessary for the Postmaster-General to curtail the facilities afforded' to private persons on occasions of public emergency.

div.head: IA HEN ZEPPS MAY BE EXPECTED.
div.p: IA HEN ZEPPS MAY BE EXPECTED.
The Barometer Rules.

Mr. James L. Fox, 104, Calabria-road, Lon- don, brother of Mrs. Henry Taylor, Manchester- road, writing to "The Times,',' says:— Sir,—As a means of forecasting future Zeppelin raids, I would point out the scientific and only method—viz., to closely watch the readings of the barometer. Every single raid over England has taken place during a period of high barometric pressure somewhere about 30.250 in., or even higher, but never has a raid occurred when the barometric reading was below 30.000 in. These high pressure conditions of the atmosphere are exactly what the gas- bags wait and long for, as the voyage out and home is more likely to be a success, for two 'reasons (1) during the high pressure conditions the aerial ocean above us is at rest, gas-bags hate wind; (2) the increased buoyancy of the air at a given height owing to the increased pressure, thus enabling them to sail at 11,000 ft. elevation with the same, ease as at 10,000ft.1 under less favourable conditions. When one comes to consider that if when on the ground the barometer registers 30.00Qin., and that if taken to a height of 10,000 ft. it registers only 19.000 in., it will be seen how important this question of pressure becomes, and as England is so close to the gas-bags' headquarters, the area of atmospheric disturbance is practically one and the same. It will be observed that the barometric readings have been eliminated from the daily papers for some time past, evidently with the object of withholding information likely to be made use of by the enemy. I say, then, when you see the barometer STEADILY rising above 30,000 in., look out for another raid. Happily such periods are rare—the rarer the better.

div.head: DYING TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: DYING TRADES COUNCIL.
Engineers And Dock Labourers'
Unions Secede.
NEW COUNCIL SUGGESTED.

Two more trade unions have followed the ex.araple of the Wiredrawers' and Bakers' Societies and withdrawn from the Warrington Trades and Labour Council owing to their hostile attitude towards the Government's com- pulsory service policy. They are the Amalgamated Society of Engineers and the National Union of Dock Labourers and Riverside Workers.

The engineers came to their decision on Mon- day, when one of the largest meetings of the local branch has ever had, was held. Mr. T. Ferguson presided. A long discussion took place, and at last it was decided to secede trom the Council, the vote being 41 to 34. The mover and seconder of the resolution were Mr. J. Craddock and Mr. G. T. Rushton. This is the third time the engineers have left the Council. Their association with them this time has been since June of last year. Their affiliatien was only decided on by a majority of five.
Council " For Trade Union Purposes."

The Warrington branch of the Dock Labourers' Union, at their meeting under the presidency Of Mr. Arthur Yates on Saturday; went so far as to suggest anew council. • The resolution they passed unanimously read: "Owing to the action of the Trades Council with reference to the Military Service Bill, and the opinions expressed at their meetings of late. we resolve to withdraw from them as at present constituted. and ask other societies for joint action in forming a trades council for purely trade union purposes.' Thiq is the Dock Labourers' second secession. The last time was owing to the Socialistic tendency of the Council. They renewed affilia- tion with them about two years ago.

div.head: 01 It "ROTTEN BOROUGH."
div.p: 01 It "ROTTEN BOROUGH."
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—At a recent meeting of the "Trades and Labour Council" Mr. Dukes, the secretiiry, said to have made a highly illuminating speech. There may be a few frivolous spirits who will venture to smile at Mr. Dukes when he says, "I have no desire to get on the Council of your rotten borough "—most people know, of Course, that he once made the attempt. Perhaps 'his discovery of the rottenness has been made since his defeat! How rotten it must be! How utterly, hope- lessly rotten to have rejected a man of such noble parts! A man with a conscience so sen- sitive that in this hour of national peril he can openly boast of his determination not. to attest! If your readers are in doubt, he gives proof of the delicacy with which his conscience is balanced, and ,of its extreme tenderness. For while he is enjoying the comparative safety and comfort of his own fireside lie is not un-, mindful of others. lie and a few kindred spirits are, in fact—to use his own choice lan- guage—" the guardians of the liberties of the men in the trenches." How reassuring this information will be to the men in the trenches! They will see "liberty enlightening the world" through the-personality of a man who has discovered a safe corner! Some will take a different view, and will be inclined to think that if the millions of Britons Who have gone forth to fight for King and country had followed the example of Mr. Dukes, the residue of " liberty" that would have re- mained as the heritage of the people, after the war, would have required a powerful microscope to discover!
NABS WOOD.

Royal Court. Searching for novelties and new numbers in pantomime is like looking for gold in one's wages, but in " Aladdin" at the Royal Court Theatre this week are several introductions both original and clover.

The skits on opera and the old-time minstrels; together with an expressively funny Russian song and dance, are items of uncommon worth, and are valuable additions to a show rarely, if over, excelled at Sir Joseph )3eecham's house.
Bruce Green as Widow Twankey is the life and soul of the "panto," for he occupies the boards practically the whole of the performance.
This talented comedian, I am informed, played in the 1912-13 pantomime at Olympia, Liver- pool, being second lead to George Formby, of "John Willie Come On" fame.

Bruce's dressing room, which I visited, re- minded me forcibly of a duchess's wardrobe, for in playing the dame he mikes fifteen distinct changes. This, with the work in 'front of the footlights, gives him an extremely busy time.

He earns a well-merited fortnight's holiday at the conclusion of this week's performance, after which he sets down to real business on the music, halls under Moss's Empires, with whom he is booked up to 1921. Bruce holds a lieutenancy in the Westminster Guards.
Miss Elsie May, the charming and gifted lady who plays Princess Badroulbadour, was for several seasons with the concert party—Harry Leslie's " Nobodys."
She has been delighting Royal Court patrons with her sweet singing and easy grace on the stage, and is a valuable acquisition to an already splendid company.
I am pleased to say that Mr. U. L. Warburton, the genial and courteous manager of the Royal Court, is making good recovery from his recent severe illness of muscular rheumatism.
Mr. A. M. Loader, the late manager, is, I believe, in charge of a large house in the land of cakes and thistles—to wit, Dundee.
Charles Locke's powerful domestic drama is being staged next week and should prove a good draw, of which more anon.

div.p: Hippodrome.

A name on the bill at the Hippodrome this week attracted one's attention, and made one realise that something of importance was one to appear at this variety theatre—" The Borstal buy," by 11. Hamilton Fyfe.
Fyfe, as is well-known, is the Russian corre- spondent for the" Daily Mail," and a music hall sketch from his pen brought expectations of a pleasure, which have been fully realised.
The sketch dealing with Cockney life in the East End is first rate, and quite in keeping with the author's reputation, and is capitally acted by John McNally and his company.
McNally tells me the following capital little story of when the sketch was first produced.
His little son, aged eight, was taken by his mother to see the first performance of "The Borstal Boy," at the Palladium, London, and after the turn, was taken into the dressing rooms.

Seeing his father he inquired when he was coming home. "Oh, little one, I have to do the show again before I can come home" re- plied his father. "Oh isn't it a nuisance, muvver," retorted the youngster, " favver mustn't be Much good or he'd 'ave done it right first time."
A vocalist of exceptional note in this week's programme is Miss Muriel George, who played with the late lamented IL G. Pellisier in the "Follies," at the Apollo Theatre, London.
Her selections from repertoire were both classical and refined, and have been greatly appreciated by musical lovers.

Next week the premier attraction is Nellie Wallace, a comedienne, who comes with a big reputation from the big centres. I don't know whether she is in Who's Who," but she is certainly "What's What!" in the music-hall world.

"Les Videos," including Leonie, who has appeared before the King, are also included in next week's programme, and their sensational turn, which created a favourable impression at the Empire and Coliseum, London, ought to be of especial interest to theatre-goers.

The screening of "The Eternal City" consti- tuted a record, and so dense was the crowd to witness the last performance that the cars were held up and hundreds of people were unable to obtain admission.
The premier film for the latter part of this week is entitled "John Glaydes' Honour," and is an adaptation of the play from the St. James' Theatre, London, in which Sir George Alexander acted.
, The staging ,is extremely fine, and is produced by one of the foremost companies of producers in the world.

Those who like the flickers of the magic lamp are promised some brilliant fare within the next week or so, for included in the boo-kings are "The Four Feathers" by A. E. W. Mason, "The White Pearl," " Zaza," " Carmen " and "Bella Donna."

The first named is to be screened next Mon- day, and should be worth seeing, for it deals With a soldier's career after he has been branded as a coward. Four white feathers have been sent him, and he redeems his character by four separate deeds of heroism.
Miss Marie Dora, who was a short time ago seen at this hall in "The Morals of Marcus,' is appearing in " The White Pearl;" the star film for the latter part of next week.
Miss Doro is world-renowned in theatreland, her principal successes being achieved in " Diplomacy " and "Milestones," both of which plays created a sensation in the Metropolis.

div.head: NEW BOOKS.
div.p: NEW BOOKS.
Kent, the Fighting Man. By George Edgar. London: Mills and Boon, Ltd.

In the opening sentence of the book the author tells us that this is the story of a man who made several false steps, but retrieved them and finally.won out in life. That the hero in work- ing out his redemption should pass through the varied stages in the career of a professional fighting man may be accounted for .by the fact that )- —.ling contests are, or were until a little while ago, a fashionable amusement, and also that the author has a predilection for this type of manliness, as witness his earlier book "The Pet of the Fancy." The two books have indeed a great resemblance to each other, though "Kent, the Fighting Man," is superior in every way to the earlier work. Mr. Edgar has written a very interesting story. The sympathy of the reader will follow the fortunes of the central figureuntil he finally redeems his character and wins the V.C. As to fighting, there is pleney of it tO be finnid in these pages. The author's descriptions are vivid in the extreme, and make exciting read- ing. It is probably a somewhat brutal sport, but if so that element is not made prominent. After all, man is a fighting animal, and the spectacle of two men striving to see which is the better will always prove attractive. The breaking out of war opens out a fresh career for the hero, and the coolness and strength and courage which had brought him fame in his earlier pursuit, now enabled him to do great service for his country and to win the V.C. As the author is careful to inform us, "this book is not a tract in disguise." We scarcely think anyone after reading it would imagine that it was so. But it clearly shows that, how- ever great the fail, strength of will and resolu- tion may retrieve the situation.

div.head: SCHOOL CHILDREN
div.p: SCHOOL CHILDREN
To Give Dramatic Account Of The War.

The scholars attending St. James' Mixed School and Fairfield Girls' School will give a dramatic account of the war in prose, poem and song in Parr Hall next Thursday, ,having been trained carefully, and with a great amount of success, by Mr.. Stansfield and Mrs. Stans- field. How exhaustively the subject will be treated by the little folk may be gathered from the following smrimary' on the official pro- gramme of "The Story We Tell" : ! The evening of Augnst 4th, 1914, finds Eng- land' awaiting the reply to the. ultimatum sent to Germany at noon. No reply comes, and the country calmly and steadfastly faces the dread situation and prays for victory. The British Navy takes up its position. Men and ships are ready. Britannia rules the waves!
The cry goes forth, "Your King and country need you." The drum beats and there is a noble and glorious response by men of all classes and of all creeds.

All parts of the Empire rush forward to help the Mother Country. THEY ARE ONE. The soldiers 'of the Empire take up their positions by the side of our Allies. Belgium makes a gallant and heroic resist- ance to the onslaught of the German hordes.

Liege. The story of Mons, and its effect on the coun- try. The demand for more men and munitions. France, with a grave yet unflinching heart, takes up the gage of battle which Germany had so haughtily thrown down. She and her Allies. England and Belgium, drive back the Prussian hordes, Which had advanced to within thirty kilometres North of Paris. Christmas in the trenches, 1914. Soldiers at war remember the message of the Prince of Peace.
The part played by Russia. Italy, aroused by \ the orator Gabriela d'Annunzio, makes common cause with the Allies.

Our gallant Prince of Wales. The part played by Warrington. The " Un- breakable Fourth" South Lameashires. The best talent at the two schools—and the talent is not limited in quantity or quality— will tell this story in reatations, songs and dance. There will be a chorus of nearly 300. The proceeds will be devoted to the Y.M.C.A.: and the Church Army Huts for Soldiers. We are glad ,to hear that the undertaking is an assured success, the sale of tickets having been most satisfactory.

Wednesday was the anniversary of the ter- mination of the Franco-German war fn 1871. That conflict was begun, like the present one, in the late summer. Irrdike the,present one, it was brought to a rapid close.
The Kaiser has already ,passed through two winters in arms. and is likely to pass' through twenty more before he reaches Paris a second time.
